atoms.title: The nuclear atom
atoms.summary: An atom is a tiny dense positive nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by a diffuse cloud of electrons.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Reach out and touch anything — a table, your own hand, a glass of water — and you are touching a structure built from atoms. The deep surprise of the atom is how *empty* it is. Nearly all the mass hides in a vanishingly small central knot called the nucleus, while the volume is filled by a thin, fast-moving haze of electrons. If the nucleus were a marble on the centre line of a football stadium, the electrons would be a faint mist out near the seats.

### Precisely
An **atom** is the smallest unit of a chemical **element** (a pure substance such as carbon or oxygen). It contains three particles:

- **protons** — charge $+1$, found in the nucleus;
- **neutrons** — charge $0$, found in the nucleus;
- **electrons** — charge $-1$, occupying the surrounding volume.

The **atomic number** $Z$ is the number of protons, and it *defines the element*. The **mass number** $A = Z + N$ counts protons plus neutrons. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Charge is measured in units of the elementary charge $e \approx 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}$; mass in atomic mass units, with the proton and neutron each near $1\ \text{u}$ and the electron about $1/1836$ of that.

Atoms of the same element that differ only in neutron count are called **isotopes**; they are chemically near-identical because chemistry depends on the electrons, which $Z$ fixes. The radius of a typical atom is around $10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ (one ångström), while the nucleus is near $10^{-15}\ \text{m}$ — a factor of $100{,}000$ smaller in radius, and so vanishingly tiny in volume that the atom is, by volume, almost entirely empty space populated only by the electron cloud.

### Worked example
Consider an atom with **6 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons**. The proton count $Z=6$ means it is **carbon**. The mass number is $A = 6 + 8 = 14$, so it is **carbon-14**. Protons ($6$) equal electrons ($6$), so the net charge is $6(+1) + 6(-1) = 0$ — a **neutral** atom. (Change the neutron count and you change the isotope, not the element.)

### Why it's true / how it works
In 1911 Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a tiny fraction bounced sharply backward. A diffuse atom could never do that; only a small, dense, positively charged core could deflect a fast particle so hard. This pinned the positive charge and almost all the mass into a nucleus roughly $10{,}000$ times smaller than the atom itself.

Before Rutherford, the prevailing "plum pudding" picture spread the positive charge smoothly through the whole atom. That model predicted alpha particles should sail through with only gentle deflections, so the rare hard backscatters were decisive: they could only come from a near head-on encounter with a concentrated charge. The fraction that bounced back, combined with the geometry of the scattering, even let physicists estimate the nucleus's size.

### Where it connects
Because the chemistry of an atom is governed by its electrons in the field of the nucleus, $Z$ is the single most important number in the whole subject — it sets the **electron configuration**, drives the **periodic table**, and underlies **effective nuclear charge**. In ordinary chemistry the nucleus never changes; only electrons rearrange.

### Watch out
Do not picture electrons as tidy planets on circular orbits. That Bohr image is a useful cartoon but physically wrong — electrons occupy fuzzy probability clouds (orbitals). Also, it is the **proton count**, not the mass or the electron count, that fixes the element's identity.

Finally, do not confuse mass number $A$ (a whole-number count of nucleons for one isotope) with the **atomic weight** on the periodic table (a decimal average over an element's natural isotope mix) — carbon's mass numbers are $12$, $13$, $14$, yet its tabulated atomic weight is about $12.011$.

depths.eli5: Everything around you is made of atoms — unimaginably tiny building blocks. Each atom has a heavy clump at its very center called the nucleus, and a cloud of much lighter specks called electrons whizzing around it. Picture a marble (the nucleus) sitting in the middle of a whole stadium, with a fuzzy swarm of tiny electrons filling all the rest of the empty space. Almost all the weight is in that central marble.
depths.core: An atom is the smallest unit of an element (a pure substance like carbon or oxygen). It is built from three kinds of particle. Protons carry a positive (+1) electric charge; neutrons carry no charge (0); electrons carry a negative (−1) charge. Protons and neutrons are packed tightly together in the central nucleus, which holds nearly all the atom's mass. Electrons occupy the much larger surrounding volume. A famous 1911 experiment by Ernest Rutherford (firing particles at thin gold foil and watching a few bounce straight back) revealed that the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a nucleus about ten-thousand times smaller than the whole atom. The number of protons — called the atomic number, written Z — defines which element you have. Neutrons add mass and tune how stable the nucleus is. Electrons are the part that does the actual chemistry.
depths.deep: Chemistry is almost entirely the behavior of the outermost electrons sitting in the electric field of the nucleus. In ordinary chemical reactions the nucleus is essentially a spectator — it never changes; only electrons are rearranged. The nucleus matters only through its charge Z, which sets how tightly the electrons are held. (Nuclear reactions, where the nucleus itself changes, are a separate subject from chemistry.)

atoms.title: Quantum numbers and orbitals
atoms.summary: Each electron is labeled by four quantum numbers that name its orbital and spin, and no two electrons in an atom share all four.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Electrons bound to an atom cannot sit just anywhere with just any energy. They are restricted to a discrete set of allowed states, each one tagged by a small set of numbers — an "address" that says roughly how far out the electron lives, what shape of region it occupies, how that region is tilted, and which way it spins. A strict rule forbids any two electrons in one atom from sharing the identical address, and that single rule is why electrons stack into layers instead of collapsing into one spot.

### Precisely
Each electron in an atom is labelled by four **quantum numbers**:

- **$n$** (principal, $n = 1,2,3,\dots$) — sets the energy and average distance from the nucleus.
- **$\ell$** (azimuthal, $0 \le \ell \le n-1$) — sets the orbital *shape*, named $s\,(\ell=0),\ p\,(1),\ d\,(2),\ f\,(3)$.
- **$m_\ell$** (magnetic, $-\ell \le m_\ell \le +\ell$) — sets the orbital's orientation in space.
- **$m_s$** (spin, $\pm\tfrac{1}{2}$) — an intrinsic two-valued property of the electron.

An **orbital** is one specific $(n,\ell,m_\ell)$ region. The **Pauli exclusion principle** states no two electrons in an atom may share all four numbers, so each orbital holds at most two electrons (with opposite spins).

### Worked example
How many electrons fit in the $n=3$ shell? The allowed subshells are $\ell = 0,1,2$, i.e. $3s, 3p, 3d$. Their orbital counts are $2\ell+1$: that is $1, 3, 5$ orbitals. Each orbital holds $2$ electrons, giving $2 + 6 + 10 = 18$ — matching the general rule $2n^2 = 2(3)^2 = 18$.

As a second check, count the orbitals in the $n=2$ shell: $\ell$ may be $0$ or $1$, giving a $2s$ ($1$ orbital) and a $2p$ ($3$ orbitals, $m_\ell=-1,0,+1$), so $4$ orbitals holding $8$ electrons — again matching $2n^2 = 2(2)^2 = 8$.

### Why it's true / how it works
The allowed shapes are not arbitrary: they are the angular solutions (spherical harmonics) of the Schrödinger equation for an electron in the nucleus's field. The radial part fixes the energy through $n$. Pauli exclusion is not a force but a consequence of electrons being identical **fermions**: swapping two of them must flip the sign of the joint wavefunction, which mathematically forbids two from occupying an identical state.

The quantization is not imposed by hand; it emerges because $\psi$ must be single-valued and well-behaved everywhere, which only happens for discrete $(n,\ell,m_\ell)$. The same boundary-condition logic that gives a guitar string its discrete harmonics gives the atom its discrete orbitals — both are standing waves confined to a region.

### Where it connects
These quantum numbers are the foundation for **electron configuration**, the structure of the **periodic table**, and the deeper **Schrödinger picture of the atom**. Subshell capacities ($s{=}2$, $p{=}6$, $d{=}10$, $f{=}14$) reappear everywhere.

### Watch out
$m_s$ does not mean the electron is literally a spinning ball — "spin" is an intrinsic quantum property with no classical equivalent. And $\ell$ is capped at $n-1$: there is no $1p$ or $2d$ orbital.

Also note that orbitals of the same $n$ but different $\ell$ (say $2s$ and $2p$) are *degenerate only in hydrogen*; in every multi-electron atom they split in energy because of shielding and penetration, which is exactly what makes the periodic table's subshell structure appear.

depths.eli5: Electrons don't sit still in fixed dots — physics describes each one by a set of four 'address' numbers that say roughly where it lives and how it spins. A strict rule says no two electrons in the same atom can have the exact same four-part address. That rule is why electrons stack up in layers instead of all piling into one spot.
depths.core: In modern physics an electron bound to a nucleus can only exist in certain allowed states, each one labeled by four 'quantum numbers' — fixed numbers that act like an address. (1) n, the principal quantum number (1, 2, 3, …), sets the electron's energy and roughly its distance from the nucleus. (2) ℓ sets the shape of the region the electron occupies; these shapes are named with letters s, p, d, f. A specific region of space an electron occupies is called an orbital. (3) m_ℓ sets the orientation of that shape in space. (4) m_s, the spin (always +½ or −½), is an intrinsic property of the electron, loosely picturable as which way it 'spins'. The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in one atom may have all four numbers identical — which is exactly why each orbital can hold at most two electrons (and only if their spins differ).
depths.deep: The allowed shapes (the ℓ values) come from the angular part of the solution to the Schrödinger equation — the master equation of quantum mechanics — and are mathematically the spherical harmonics; the radial part (linked to n) fixes the energy. Pauli exclusion is not an extra force pushing electrons apart but a deep consequence of electrons being identical 'fermions': the combined wavefunction describing two of them must flip sign if you swap them, which mathematically forbids them sharing an identical state.

atoms.title: Electron configuration
atoms.summary: Ground-state electrons fill orbitals from lowest energy up, one spin-paired pair at a time, following Aufbau, Hund, and Pauli.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Picture an atom's orbitals as theatre seats priced by how close they are to the stage (the nucleus). Electrons fill the cheapest seats first. When several seats cost the same, electrons spread out one per seat before doubling up — and no two ever take the identical seat. Carrying this out for all an atom's electrons gives its **electron configuration**, a compact map of where every electron sits.

### Precisely
The **electron configuration** lists the occupied orbitals of an atom in its lowest-energy (ground) state, built from three rules:

- **Aufbau principle** — add electrons to the lowest-available-energy orbital first.
- **Hund's rule** — within a set of equal-energy (degenerate) orbitals, singly occupy each with parallel spins before pairing.
- **Pauli exclusion** — never two electrons in the identical state.

The approximate filling order is $1s\,2s\,2p\,3s\,3p\,4s\,3d\,4p\,5s\,4d\,5p\dots$ Notation gives each subshell a superscript of its electron count.

### Worked example
**Oxygen**, $Z=8$. Fill in order: $1s^2$ (2), $2s^2$ (4 total), then $2p^4$ (8 total). So oxygen is $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^4$. By Hund's rule the four $2p$ electrons occupy the three $2p$ orbitals as $\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow$ — **two unpaired electrons**, which is why $\mathrm{O_2}$ turns out magnetic.

For a slightly harder case, **iron** ($Z=26$) is $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2\,3d^6$. When it forms $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, the $4s$ electrons leave *first* (not the last-written $3d$), giving $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6$ — a rule that surprises students but follows from $3d$ sinking below $4s$ once occupied.

### Why it's true / how it works
Orbital energies are not ordered strictly by $n$. The $4s$ orbital fills before $3d$ because $4s$ **penetrates** closer to the nucleus and is **shielded** less. Once $3d$ is occupied it often drops below $4s$, which is why transition metals lose $4s$ electrons first when ionising. A few elements (Cr: $[\text{Ar}]4s^1 3d^5$; Cu: $[\text{Ar}]4s^1 3d^{10}$) break the simple pattern because half-filled and filled subshells gain extra **exchange** stability.

Exchange energy is a purely quantum stabilization that grows with the number of pairs of *parallel-spin* electrons in degenerate orbitals; a half-filled $d^5$ or $p^3$ set maximizes those parallel pairs, which is why chromium and copper borrow a single $s$ electron to reach the extra-stable half- or fully-filled $d$ shell.

### Where it connects
Configurations explain the **blocks** of the **periodic table** ($s$, $p$, $d$, $f$), the **valence** electrons that drive bonding, and **periodic trends**. The noble-gas shorthand (e.g. $[\text{Ne}]$) compresses inner shells.

### Watch out
Don't blindly write $3d$ before $4s$ from the $n$ value alone — energy ordering, not $n$, controls filling. And when an atom ionises, remove the highest-$n$ electrons ($4s$) first, not the last ones written.

Writing the configuration in filling order is fine, but for ionization always reorder by principal quantum number and strip the highest-$n$ electrons first — the single most common mistake in transition-metal chemistry.

depths.eli5: Think of an atom's orbitals (the regions electrons live in) as seats in a theater priced by how close they are to the front. Electrons fill the cheapest seats first. When several seats cost the same, electrons spread out — one to each — before any seat is shared. And no two ever share an identical seat. Doing this for an atom's electrons gives you its 'electron configuration', a shorthand for where all its electrons sit.
depths.core: An electron configuration lists which orbitals an atom's electrons occupy in its lowest-energy (ground) state. You build it with three rules. The Aufbau principle ('building-up'): add electrons one at a time to the lowest-energy orbital still available. Hund's rule: when several orbitals have the same energy (called 'degenerate'), put one electron in each, all spinning the same way, before doubling any up — this keeps electrons apart and lowers repulsion. The Pauli exclusion principle: never put two electrons in the identical state. Writing configurations this way explains the periodic table's 'blocks' — the s-block, p-block, the d-block (the transition metals), and the f-block — each block being the orbital type being filled there.
depths.deep: Orbital energies aren't ordered strictly by the number n. The 4s orbital fills before 3d because of 'penetration' (4s dips closer to the nucleus) and 'shielding' (inner electrons partly block the nuclear pull). Once 3d is occupied it often sinks below 4s in energy, which is why transition-metal ions lose their 4s electrons first when they form ions. A few elements (chromium, copper) break the simple pattern because a half-filled or completely filled subshell gains extra stability from a quantum effect called exchange energy.

atoms.title: The periodic table as organizing law
atoms.summary: Arranging elements by atomic number makes chemical properties recur periodically, because outer-shell structure repeats.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
There are about 118 known elements. Line them up in order of proton count and something striking happens: chemical behaviour starts to repeat. Every so often you hit an element that behaves like an earlier one — a chemical "cousin". Fold that line into rows so cousins stack into columns, and you have the periodic table: a map where an element's neighbourhood tells you how it acts.

### Precisely
The **periodic table** arranges all elements so that chemical properties recur **periodically**. Modern tables order strictly by **atomic number** $Z$. A **group** is a column; a **period** is a row. Elements in the same group share the same outer-shell (**valence**) electron arrangement, and since valence electrons control bonding, same-group elements react alike. The table divides into **blocks** — $s$, $p$, $d$ (transition metals), $f$ (lanthanides/actinides) — named for the subshell being filled.

### Worked example
Compare **sodium** ($Z=11$, $[\text{Ne}]3s^1$) and **potassium** ($Z=19$, $[\text{Ar}]4s^1$). Both sit in Group 1 with a single $s$ valence electron. Predictably, both are soft, highly reactive metals that lose that one electron to form $+1$ ions and react vigorously with water. The shared *valence pattern*, not the total electron count, explains the family resemblance.

The halogens (Group 17) make the same point from the nonmetal side: fluorine ($[\text{He}]2s^22p^5$) and chlorine ($[\text{Ne}]3s^23p^5$) each have seven valence electrons, each one short of a full octet, so both are aggressive electron-grabbers that form $-1$ ions and react explosively with reactive metals.

### Why it's true / how it works
Period lengths ($2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32$) exactly equal the electrons the subshells filled in each row can hold. The block structure mirrors which orbital type ($\ell$) the most-recently-added electron occupies. In short, the periodic law is the solutions of the Schrödinger equation made visible: chemistry repeats because electron configurations repeat.

This is why Mendeleev's gaps were so persuasive: he predicted the properties of "eka-silicon" (later found as germanium) from the elements above and below its empty slot, and the match was striking — the table was not just a filing system but a predictive law years before quantum mechanics explained *why*.

### Where it connects
The table is the organising chart for **periodic trends**, **effective nuclear charge**, and every kind of **bonding**. Mendeleev's genius (1869) was leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and predicting their properties from position alone.

### Watch out
Order is by $Z$ (proton count), *not* atomic mass — a few pairs like Ar/K and Te/I would be misordered by mass. And group similarity is about valence-shell structure, so it is strongest in the main groups; transition metals show richer, less uniform behaviour.

One more subtlety: hydrogen sits awkwardly. It has a single $s$ electron like the alkali metals but behaves nothing like them, which is why many tables float it apart — a reminder that position encodes valence structure, not a guarantee of identical chemistry.

depths.eli5: There are about 118 known elements (the pure substances everything is made of). If you line them up in order of how many protons they have, something magical happens: their behavior starts to repeat in a regular pattern. Every so often you reach an element that acts a lot like an earlier one — a chemical 'cousin'. The periodic table is just that line-up, folded into rows so the cousins stack into columns.
depths.core: The periodic table arranges all the elements so that chemical behavior recurs in a regular ('periodic') way. The 19th-century chemist Dmitri Mendeleev first ordered elements so that families with similar reactivity fell in the same column, even leaving gaps for elements not yet discovered. The modern table orders strictly by atomic number Z (proton count). A column is called a group; a row is called a period. The repeating behavior is a direct shadow of electron configuration: elements in the same group have the same arrangement of outer electrons (their 'valence' electrons), and since outer electrons control bonding, same-group elements react alike.
depths.deep: The table is essentially a map of the solutions to the Schrödinger equation. The length of each period (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32) exactly equals the number of electrons the subshells being filled there can hold. The block structure (s, p, d, f) corresponds to which orbital-shape (the ℓ value) the most recently added electron occupies. In other words, the periodic law is quantum mechanics made visible on a wall chart.

atoms.title: Periodic trends
atoms.summary: Atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, and electronegativity vary smoothly across periods and down groups.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Because the table is so orderly, properties change smoothly as you move through it. Across a row, atoms shrink and grip their electrons more tightly. Down a column, atoms swell and hold outer electrons more loosely. Learn those two directions and you can predict how an element behaves without memorising each one.

### Precisely
The main **periodic trends**:

- **Atomic radius** — size of the atom.
- **Ionization energy** — energy to remove an electron, $\mathrm{X}(g)\to\mathrm{X}^+(g)+e^-$.
- **Electron affinity** — energy released on gaining an electron.
- **Electronegativity** — pull on shared bonding electrons.

**Across a period (left→right):** radius **decreases**; ionization energy and electronegativity **increase**. **Down a group:** radius **increases**; ionization energy **decreases**. The driver is **effective nuclear charge** $Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - S$.

### Worked example
Which has the higher first ionization energy, **sodium** or **chlorine**? Both are in Period 3, but Cl ($Z=17$) sits far right of Na ($Z=11$). Across the period $Z$ rises while the added electrons share the same shell and shield poorly, so $Z_{\text{eff}}$ climbs. Chlorine therefore holds its electrons more tightly — **chlorine** has the higher ionization energy.

Compare sizes instead: going down Group 1 from lithium to caesium, each element adds a new electron shell, so atomic radius grows steadily even though nuclear charge rises — the new outer shell sits farther from the nucleus than the added proton can pull it in.

### Why it's true / how it works
Across a period, each step adds a proton ($Z{+}1$) and an electron to the *same* shell, which shields weakly, so $Z_{\text{eff}}$ grows and pulls the shell inward. Down a group, each step adds a whole new outer shell, so the valence electrons are farther out and easier to remove. Telling exceptions — small dips at boron and oxygen in ionization energy — directly expose subshell and electron-pairing energetics.

Electronegativity, electron affinity, and ionization energy all rise toward the top-right because they all track how tightly the nucleus grips electrons, i.e. $Z_{\text{eff}}$ — which is why fluorine (top-right of the reactive nonmetals) is the most electronegative element and the noble gases, with full shells, barely react at all.

### Where it connects
These trends predict which atoms donate electrons (→ **ionic bonding**) and which accept them, and they feed directly into **electronegativity and polarity**. They are the periodic table's predictive payoff.

### Watch out
"Bigger atom" does not mean "more protons wins" — down a group $Z$ rises yet atoms get *bigger*, because added shells outweigh the stronger nucleus. Always reason through $Z_{\text{eff}}$ and shell count, not raw $Z$ alone.

Cations are always *smaller* than their parent atoms (losing a shell or reducing repulsion) and anions are *larger* — so don't assume an ion keeps its neutral atom's size when reasoning about lattice energies or solubility.

depths.eli5: Because the periodic table is so orderly, an element's properties change smoothly as you move across it. As you go left-to-right across a row, atoms get a little smaller and hold onto their electrons more tightly. As you go down a column, atoms get bigger and hold their outer electrons more loosely. Knowing these two simple directions lets you guess how an element behaves without memorizing each one.
depths.core: Periodic trends are the smooth changes in atomic properties across the table. The key ones: atomic radius (how big the atom is), ionization energy (how hard it is to pull an electron off), electron affinity (how much energy is released when the atom grabs an extra electron), and electronegativity (how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons in a bond). Across a period, the nuclear charge (proton count) grows but the electrons are being added to the same outer shell, so the nucleus pulls everything in tighter: atoms shrink and ionization energy and electronegativity rise. Down a group, each step adds a whole new shell of electrons farther out, so the outermost electrons are easier to remove. These trends predict which atoms tend to give electrons away and which tend to take them — the heart of how bonds form.
depths.deep: The single quantity behind all these trends is the effective nuclear charge, Z_eff = Z − S: the net pull an outer electron actually feels once inner electrons (the 'shielding' S) partly cancel the nuclear charge Z. The trends have telling exceptions where subshell stability matters — for example the small dips in ionization energy at boron (after the 2s subshell just filled) and oxygen (after the 2p subshell became half-filled) directly reveal the underlying electron-pairing and exchange energetics.

atoms.title: Effective nuclear charge
atoms.summary: An outer electron feels not the full nuclear charge but a reduced charge, screened by inner electrons.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
The nucleus tugs on every electron, but an outer electron never feels the full tug. Inner electrons crowd between it and the nucleus, partly blocking the pull — like people in front of you at a concert blocking your view of the stage. So the outer electron experiences a watered-down nuclear pull.

### Precisely
$$Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - S$$
where $Z$ is the nuclear charge (proton count) and $S$ is the **shielding** (screening) constant — the portion of $Z$ cancelled by repulsion from other electrons. $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is the *net* charge a given electron actually feels, and it controls atomic size, ionization energy, and electronegativity.

### Worked example
For a valence electron of **sodium** ($Z=11$, $[\text{Ne}]3s^1$), the ten inner electrons shield strongly. A crude estimate $S \approx 10$ gives $Z_{\text{eff}} \approx 11 - 10 = 1$. The lone $3s$ electron feels only about a $+1$ pull — which is exactly why sodium gives it up so readily to form $\mathrm{Na}^+$. (Slater's rules refine $S$ to about $8.5$, giving $Z_{\text{eff}}\approx 2.5$, still far below the bare $11$.)

Contrast that with **chlorine** ($Z=17$, $[\text{Ne}]3s^23p^5$): again ten inner electrons shield, so $Z_{\text{eff}} \approx 17 - 10 = 7$ for a valence electron — far higher than sodium's $\approx 1$. That large $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is why chlorine, in the same period, holds and attracts electrons so much more strongly than sodium.

### Why it's true / how it works
Shielding is imperfect and depends on orbital shape because of **penetration**: $s$ electrons dip close to the nucleus and shield well, $p$ less, $d$ and $f$ poorly, so $s>p>d>f$. This penetration ordering splits subshells of the same $n$ into slightly different energies — which is precisely why orbitals fill in their characteristic order.

Slater's rules formalize the penetration ordering: electrons in the same group shield by $0.35$ each, inner-shell ($n-1$) electrons by $0.85$, and deeper electrons by a full $1.00$ — a crude but surprisingly effective recipe that reproduces the observed sizes and ionization energies across a period.

### Where it connects
$Z_{\text{eff}}$ is the single quantity behind all **periodic trends** and the order of **electron configuration** filling. Slater's rules give a hand recipe for $S$.

Conceptually it is the quiet workhorse of the early curriculum: nearly every "why" question about atomic size, ionization energy, and electronegativity ultimately reduces to how $Z_{\text{eff}}$ changes, making it one of the highest-leverage ideas to truly internalize before tackling bonding.

### Watch out
Shielding is not all-or-nothing: an electron is only partly screened, and electrons in the *same* shell shield each other weakly (they don't get fully "in front"). That weak same-shell shielding is exactly why $Z_{\text{eff}}$ rises across a period.

Because the effect is graded, never assume $S$ equals the simple count of inner electrons — same-shell electrons contribute partial, not full, screening, and that partial term is precisely what lets $Z_{\text{eff}}$ climb steadily from left to right.

depths.eli5: The nucleus tugs on every electron, but the outer electrons don't feel the full tug. The electrons packed in close to the nucleus form a crowd that partly blocks the pull — like people standing in front of you at a concert blocking your view of the stage. So an outer electron feels a watered-down version of the nucleus's pull. The equation Z_eff = Z − S just says: real felt pull = full charge minus the blocking.
depths.core: An atom's nucleus has a charge Z (equal to its number of protons), but an outer electron doesn't experience all of it. The inner-shell electrons repel the outer electron and partly cancel the nuclear pull — an effect called shielding, written S. The leftover pull the outer electron actually feels is the effective nuclear charge: Z_eff = Z − S. This one quantity explains a lot at once: how big atoms are, how much energy it takes to remove an electron (ionization energy), and why, moving across a period, the outer electrons get harder and harder to pull off (Z rises faster than S).
depths.deep: Shielding is imperfect and depends on orbital shape: s electrons 'penetrate' closer to the nucleus and shield well, p electrons less, d and f electrons poorly. Slater's rules are a simple recipe for estimating S by hand. The penetration ordering s > p > d > f is exactly why subshells within the same shell end up at slightly different energies, which in turn drives the order in which orbitals fill.

atoms.title: Ionic bonding
atoms.summary: A metal donates electrons to a nonmetal, and the resulting oppositely charged ions are held in a lattice by electrostatics.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Atoms can stick together in several ways; this is one. One atom simply hands its spare outer electrons to a neighbour. The giver is now short of electrons (positive) and the taker has extra (negative). Opposite charges attract, so the two cling together hard, and countless such pairs stack into a rigid crystal. Table salt is held together exactly this way.

### Precisely
In an **ionic bond**, electrons transfer completely from one atom to another. It forms between an atom of **low ionization energy** (a metal) and one of **high electron affinity** (a nonmetal). The electron-loser becomes a positive **cation**; the gainer a negative **anion**. Vast numbers of ions assemble into a **crystal lattice**. The energy released in forming that lattice from gaseous ions is the **lattice energy**, scaling roughly as
$$E_{\text{lattice}} \propto \frac{q_1 q_2}{r},$$
the product of ion charges over their separation.

### Worked example
Sodium ($[\text{Ne}]3s^1$) loses one electron to chlorine ($[\text{Ne}]3s^23p^5$):
$$\mathrm{Na} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^+Cl^-}.$$
Na becomes $\mathrm{Na^+}$ (a stable neon configuration); Cl becomes $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ (a stable argon configuration). The ions stack into a cubic lattice of alternating $+$ and $-$, giving a hard, brittle solid melting near $801\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

You can also see the energetics as a cycle (a Born–Haber cycle): vaporizing and ionizing sodium *costs* energy, and even forming $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ from $\mathrm{Cl}$ releases only modest energy — the reaction is downhill overall *only* because the huge lattice energy released when the ions assemble into the crystal more than pays for all those steps.

### Why it's true / how it works
Because lattice energy scales with $q_1 q_2/r$, **charge magnitude dominates**: $\mathrm{MgO}$ (ions $2+$ and $2-$) has a far larger product than $\mathrm{NaCl}$ ($1+$, $1-$), so MgO melts near $2850\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ versus NaCl's $801\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The Born–Landé equation makes this precise.

The $q_1q_2/r$ dependence also explains *size* effects: small ions sit closer together (smaller $r$), so lithium salts often have larger lattice energies than the corresponding heavier-alkali salts, all else equal. This is the same Coulomb law that governs every electrostatic interaction in chemistry.

### Where it connects
Ionic bonding sits at the high-electronegativity-difference end of the continuum described in **electronegativity and polarity**, opposite **covalent** and **metallic** bonding. It rests on **periodic trends** (who gives, who takes).

### Watch out
"Purely ionic" is an idealisation — real bonds always have some covalent (shared) character, which grows when a small, highly charged cation distorts a large anion's cloud (Fajans' rules). Ionic solids conduct only when **molten or dissolved**, never as dry solids, because the ions must be free to move.

Don't picture an ionic compound as discrete "$\mathrm{NaCl}$ molecules" — there is no single Na bonded to one particular Cl. The formula gives the *ratio* of ions in an extended lattice, where each $\mathrm{Na^+}$ is surrounded by six $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ and vice versa.

Now the giver is short of electrons (positively charged) and the taker has extra (negatively charged). Opposite charges attract, so the two stick together hard. Table salt is held together exactly this way.
depths.core: A bond is the force that holds atoms together in a substance. In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred completely from one atom to another. This happens when an atom that gives up electrons easily (low ionization energy — typically a metal) meets one that grabs electrons readily (high electron affinity — typically a nonmetal). An atom that has lost electrons becomes a positively charged ion called a cation; one that has gained electrons becomes a negatively charged anion. Vast numbers of these ions stack into a regular, repeating 3-D pattern called a crystal lattice, with positives and negatives alternating. The total energy released by assembling that lattice is the lattice energy — the glue's strength. Ionic compounds are hard, brittle, and melt only at high temperatures; they conduct electricity only when melted or dissolved (when the ions are free to move).
depths.deep: Lattice energy scales roughly as q₁q₂/r — the product of the ion charges divided by their separation (Coulomb's law, made precise by the Born–Landé equation). So charge magnitude dominates: magnesium oxide (with 2+ and 2− ions) melts far higher than sodium chloride (1+ and 1−) even though the ions are similar in size. 'Purely ionic' is an idealization; real bonds always have some shared-electron (covalent) character, which grows when a small, highly charged cation distorts a large anion's electron cloud (summarized by Fajans' rules).

quiz.answer: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, quantified as the lattice energy.

atoms.title: Covalent bonding
atoms.summary: Two atoms share electron pairs, lowering energy by letting electrons feel both nuclei at once.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Here is the other main way atoms bind. Instead of one atom handing electrons over, two atoms hold a pair of electrons in the gap between them — like two children gripping the same rope. That shared pair is pulled toward both nuclei at once, drawing the atoms together. Most molecules in living things — water, sugar, DNA — are built from bonds like this.

### Precisely
In a **covalent bond**, two atoms **share** one or more electron pairs rather than transferring them. It forms when neither atom can easily lose or gain electrons outright — typically between nonmetals. A shared pair between the nuclei is attracted to both, lowering the system's energy. Atoms tend to share until each reaches a full outer shell, usually eight (the **octet rule**; hydrogen needs two). The **bond order** counts shared pairs: $1$ = single, $2$ = double, $3$ = triple. Higher bond order means shorter, stronger bonds.

### Worked example
Two hydrogen atoms, each with one $1s$ electron, approach. As their electron clouds overlap, electron density piles up *between* the nuclei. The total energy falls to a minimum at a separation of about $74\ \text{pm}$ — the bond length — releasing roughly $436\ \text{kJ/mol}$, the bond energy. Pull the atoms closer and nuclear repulsion shoots the energy back up; pull them apart and you must pay that $436\ \text{kJ/mol}$ to break the bond.

Bond order shows up clearly in nitrogen: $\mathrm{N_2}$ has a **triple** bond (three shared pairs), making it both very short ($\sim 110\ \text{pm}$) and extraordinarily strong ($\sim 945\ \text{kJ/mol}$). That strength is exactly why nitrogen gas is so inert and why releasing it is what makes many explosives so energetic.

### Why it's true / how it works
The energy drop is genuinely quantum-mechanical. The two atomic electron "waves" add constructively, concentrating density between the nuclei. The dominant reason energy falls is that the shared electron **delocalises** over both atoms, lowering its kinetic energy. More shared pairs raise the bond order, giving the shorter, stronger bonds seen in double and triple bonds.

A potential-energy curve captures the whole story: far apart, the atoms barely interact; as they approach, the shared-electron attraction lowers the energy into a well; push too close and nucleus–nucleus repulsion sends it steeply upward. The bottom of the well is the equilibrium bond length, and its depth is the bond energy.

### Where it connects
Covalent bonding underlies **Lewis structures**, **VSEPR** geometry, **hybridization**, **molecular orbital theory**, and all of organic chemistry's **functional groups**. It is the middle of the bonding continuum in **electronegativity and polarity**.

### Watch out
"Sharing" rarely means *equal* sharing — when the two atoms differ in electronegativity the pair sits closer to one, giving a polar bond. And the octet rule is a guideline, not a law: $\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{NO}$, and $\mathrm{SF_6}$ all break it.

A common confusion: covalent compounds are often gases, liquids, or low-melting solids, but that softness reflects weak forces *between* molecules, not weak covalent bonds *within* them — the internal bonds are typically very strong.

That shared pair tugs on both atoms at once and pulls them together. Most of the molecules in living things (water, sugar, DNA) are built from bonds like this.

Atoms tend to keep sharing until each reaches a stable, full count of outer electrons — usually eight, the 'octet rule'. Sharing one pair gives a single bond, two pairs a double bond, three pairs a triple bond. More shared pairs make a shorter, stronger bond.

atoms.title: Electronegativity and bond polarity
atoms.summary: Unequal electron-attracting power between bonded atoms creates partial charges and a continuum from covalent to ionic.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
When two atoms share electrons, they rarely share fairly. One usually pulls the shared pair closer. The stronger puller ends up slightly negative, the weaker one slightly positive — so even a shared bond can have a "plus end" and a "minus end," like a tiny magnet.

### Precisely
**Electronegativity** measures how strongly an atom attracts the electrons in a bond (Pauling's scale runs from about $0.7$ for caesium to $4.0$ for fluorine). Compare the two atoms in a bond:

- nearly equal → **nonpolar covalent** (even sharing);
- moderate difference → **polar covalent**, with partial charges $\delta-$ on the stronger puller and $\delta+$ on the other;
- very large difference → **ionic** (a complete grab).

Whole-molecule polarity is the **dipole moment** $\mu = q\,d$ (charge times separation), a vector that depends on geometry.

### Worked example
**Carbon dioxide**, $\mathrm{O{=}C{=}O}$. Each $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ bond is strongly polar ($\Delta\chi \approx 1.0$), with oxygen $\delta-$ and carbon $\delta+$. Yet the molecule is **linear**, so the two bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel: $\vec{\mu}_{\text{net}} = \vec{0}$. CO$_2$ has polar bonds but **no net dipole** — geometry overrides bond polarity.

Contrast water, $\mathrm{H_2O}$: it has two polar $\mathrm{O{-}H}$ bonds like CO$_2$ has two polar bonds, but water is **bent**, so its bond dipoles do *not* cancel and add to a substantial net dipole — which is exactly why water is such a good solvent for ionic and polar substances.

### Why it's true / how it works
The covalent-to-ionic change is a smooth continuum, not two boxes, which is why we use a numeric scale derived from measured bond energies. A molecule's net dipole is the vector sum of its bond dipoles; symmetric arrangements (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral with identical groups) cancel, while bent or pyramidal ones (water, ammonia) do not.

Pauling built his scale from bond energies: a purely covalent bond's energy should be the average of the two pure-element bonds, and the *excess* energy of the real bond reflects its ionic (polar) character. The bigger the electronegativity gap, the larger that excess, which is how a single number captures "unequal sharing."

### Where it connects
Bond polarity governs **intermolecular forces**, solubility, and where a molecule reacts; it underlies **oxidation states** and the reactivity logic of **functional groups**. It builds directly on **periodic trends** and **covalent bonding**.

Looking ahead, the partial charges this concept introduces are the seeds of nearly all reactivity: a $\delta+$ carbon is where nucleophiles strike, and a $\delta-$ oxygen is where electrophiles and hydrogen bonds latch on, so polarity quietly organizes the whole landscape of organic and biological chemistry.

### Watch out
The classic trap: assuming polar bonds always give a polar molecule. CO$_2$ proves otherwise. Always check the **shape** (via VSEPR) before deciding whether bond dipoles cancel.

Distinguish bond polarity (a property of one bond) from molecular polarity (the vector sum over all bonds and lone pairs) — CO$_2$ proves they can disagree. Always settle the geometry first.

The stronger puller ends up a little bit negative (it has the electrons more), and the weaker one ends up a little bit positive. So even a shared bond can have a 'plus end' and a 'minus end' — like a tiny magnet.

Compare the two atoms in a bond: if their electronegativities are nearly equal, they share evenly — a nonpolar covalent bond. If one pulls noticeably harder, the electrons sit closer to it, giving a polar bond with small partial charges, written δ− (slightly negative) on the stronger puller and δ+ (slightly positive) on the other. If the difference is huge, the pull becomes a complete grab — that's an ionic bond. So electronegativity difference is a sliding scale from nonpolar, to polar, to ionic. Bond polarity controls a molecule's solubility, the weak attractions between molecules, and where it tends to react.
depths.deep: Because the covalent-to-ionic change is a smooth continuum, not two separate categories, chemists use scales like Pauling's (derived from measured bond energies). Polarity at the whole-molecule level is captured by the dipole moment, μ = q·d (charge times separation), which depends on geometry. A molecule can have polar bonds yet be nonpolar overall if those bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel — carbon dioxide (CO₂) is the classic example because it is linear.

atoms.title: Lewis structures and the octet rule
atoms.summary: Dot-and-line diagrams track valence electrons as bonds and lone pairs, with most main-group atoms seeking eight.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Chemists sketch molecules with a simple bookkeeping diagram. Draw each atom's outer electrons as dots, pair them up — a shared pair becomes a line (a bond) — and arrange things so every atom is surrounded by a full set, usually eight. This sketch, a **Lewis structure**, shows how the atoms connect and where the lone electrons sit.

### Precisely
A **Lewis structure** tracks an atom's **valence** electrons as **bonding pairs** (lines, shared between two atoms) and **lone pairs** (dots on a single atom). Most main-group atoms obey the **octet rule** (eight valence electrons); hydrogen takes two. When several drawings are possible, **formal charge** — comparing an atom's assigned electrons to its free-atom count — picks the best one. **Resonance** is used when electrons are genuinely delocalised over equivalent arrangements.

$$\text{formal charge} = (\text{valence } e^-) - (\text{lone-pair } e^-) - \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{bonding } e^-)$$

### Worked example
**Carbon dioxide.** Valence electrons: $\mathrm{C}\,(4) + 2\times\mathrm{O}\,(6) = 16$. Arrange as $\mathrm{O{=}C{=}O}$: two $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ double bonds use $8$ electrons; the remaining $8$ become two lone pairs on each oxygen. Now check octets — carbon: $4$ bonds $= 8\,e^-$ ✓; each oxygen: $2$ bonds $+ 2$ lone pairs $= 8\,e^-$ ✓. Formal charges are all zero, confirming this is the best structure.

**Ozone** ($\mathrm{O_3}$) needs **resonance**: you can draw the double bond on the left or the right, and neither single picture is correct. The real molecule is a blend, with both oxygen–oxygen bonds identical and of order $1.5$ — a delocalization that Lewis dots can only hint at by drawing both structures.

### Why it's true / how it works
The octet rule works because an atom's outer $s$ and $p$ orbitals together hold eight electrons — a full, low-energy set. But it is a rule of thumb, not law. Real exceptions: electron-deficient $\mathrm{BF_3}$ (six around B), odd-electron radicals like $\mathrm{NO}$, and "expanded octets" like $\mathrm{SF_6}$ (twelve around S), now explained by very polar bonding rather than $d$-orbital filling.

Formal charge is the tie-breaker: the best Lewis structure minimizes formal charges and places any negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom. This is why, for example, the connectivity of cyanate ($\mathrm{OCN^-}$) is preferred with the charge on oxygen rather than nitrogen.

### Where it connects
Lewis structures are the launchpad for **VSEPR** (shape), **hybridization**, and **oxidation states**. Resonance previews delocalisation, fully treated in **molecular orbital theory**.

### Watch out
Count *all* valence electrons first and conserve them — the commonest error is adding or losing electrons mid-drawing. And don't force an octet where chemistry forbids it (B, Be, expanded-octet centres). Use formal charge to choose among valid skeletons.

Resonance structures are *not* fast-flipping real forms — the molecule does not oscillate between them. They are two incomplete sketches whose average is the single, static, delocalized real structure.

atoms.title: VSEPR and molecular geometry
atoms.summary: Electron-pair domains around a central atom repel and spread out, fixing molecular shape.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Molecules have definite 3-D shapes, and shape decides behaviour. The trick to predicting it: around the central atom, each clump of electrons repels every other clump, so they spread out as far apart as they can — exactly like balloons tied at one knot pushing apart. Wherever the clumps point is the molecule's shape.

### Precisely
**VSEPR** (Valence-Shell Electron-Pair Repulsion): count the **electron domains** around a central atom, where each bonded group (single, double, or triple) and each **lone pair** counts as one domain. Domains arrange to maximise separation:

- $2$ domains → **linear**, $180^\circ$;
- $3$ → **trigonal planar**, $120^\circ$;
- $4$ → **tetrahedral**, $109.5^\circ$;
- $5$ → **trigonal bipyramidal**;
- $6$ → **octahedral**, $90^\circ$.

Lone pairs occupy more space than bonds, so they compress bond angles.

### Worked example
**Water**, $\mathrm{H_2O}$. Oxygen has $2$ bonding domains (to H) plus $2$ lone pairs $= 4$ domains, so the base geometry is **tetrahedral**. But only two positions hold atoms, so the *molecular* shape is **bent**. The two lone pairs repel more strongly than the bonds, squeezing the H–O–H angle from the ideal $109.5^\circ$ down to the observed $104.5^\circ$.

**Ammonia** ($\mathrm{NH_3}$) is the parallel case: nitrogen has three bonds plus one lone pair ($4$ domains, tetrahedral base), giving a *trigonal pyramidal* molecular shape with H–N–H angles compressed to about $107^\circ$ by the single lone pair — between water's $104.5^\circ$ (two lone pairs) and methane's ideal $109.5^\circ$ (none).

### Why it's true / how it works
VSEPR predicts shapes beautifully from a simple electron count, but it is a model, not the cause. The deeper reason domains avoid each other is the **Pauli principle** (same-spin electrons cannot share a state) plus plain electrostatic repulsion. Lone pairs sit closer to the central atom and are more diffuse, hence their stronger squeeze.

The lone-pair-squeeze ordering — lone pair–lone pair repulsion $>$ lone pair–bond $>$ bond–bond — falls straight out of where the electron density sits: a lone pair is held by only one nucleus and so spreads wider and closer in, pushing harder on its neighbors than a bonding pair pinned between two nuclei.

### Where it connects
VSEPR pairs naturally with **hybridization** (which names the orbitals pointing in those directions) and with **electronegativity and polarity** (geometry decides whether bond dipoles cancel). It builds on **Lewis structures**.

### Watch out
Count domains, not atoms: a double bond is *one* domain, and lone pairs count too. The geometry name refers to the *atom positions* (so $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is "bent," not "tetrahedral"), even though the electron arrangement is tetrahedral.

For five and six domains, lone pairs prefer specific positions (the equatorial sites in a trigonal bipyramid) to minimize repulsion — so molecules like $\mathrm{SF_4}$ and $\mathrm{ClF_3}$ have distinctive "see-saw" and "T" shapes you cannot guess from domain count alone.

atoms.title: Orbital hybridization
atoms.summary: Atomic orbitals mix into equivalent hybrid orbitals that point toward bonding partners, matching observed geometry.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
An atom's basic electron "rooms" (orbitals) come in different shapes and don't all point the right way for bonding. So the atom blends them into a fresh set of identical, evenly spaced rooms aimed straight at its neighbours. With matching rooms pointing the right directions, the bonds come out equal and the molecule takes on a clean, symmetric shape.

### Precisely
**Hybridization** mixes an atom's atomic orbitals into equivalent **hybrid orbitals** directed at its bonding partners:

- **$sp^3$** — one $s$ + three $p$ → four hybrids in a tetrahedron ($109.5^\circ$);
- **$sp^2$** — one $s$ + two $p$ → three hybrids in a plane ($120^\circ$), leaving one unmixed $p$ for a $\pi$ bond;
- **$sp$** — one $s$ + one $p$ → two hybrids in a line ($180^\circ$), leaving two unmixed $p$ orbitals.

A normal end-on overlap gives a **$\sigma$ bond**; a side-on overlap of leftover $p$ orbitals gives a **$\pi$ bond**.

### Worked example
**Ethene**, $\mathrm{C_2H_4}$. Each carbon is **$sp^2$**: three $sp^2$ hybrids form $\sigma$ bonds (two C–H and one C–C), all at $120^\circ$ in a plane. The unmixed $p$ orbital on each carbon, perpendicular to that plane, overlaps side-on with its partner to form the second bond — the **$\pi$ bond** of the $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ double bond. So $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ is one $\sigma$ plus one $\pi$, and the molecule is flat with restricted rotation.

**Acetylene** ($\mathrm{C_2H_2}$) takes it further: each carbon is $sp$ (two hybrids, $180^\circ$), leaving *two* unmixed $p$ orbitals per carbon that form *two* $\pi$ bonds — so the $\mathrm{C{\equiv}C}$ triple bond is one $\sigma$ plus two $\pi$, and the molecule is rod-straight and linear.

### Why it's true / how it works
Hybridization is a mathematical re-description: the combination of atomic orbitals that best matches the molecule's symmetry. It conveniently splits bonding into a $\sigma$ framework (from hybrids) and a $\pi$ system (from leftover $p$ orbitals). It is descriptive, not predictive — photoelectron spectroscopy shows the underlying orbitals aren't all truly identical.

The $s$-character of a hybrid sets its shape and even the bond angles and acidity: more $s$-character ($sp$, $50\%$) holds electrons closer to the nucleus than $sp^3$ ($25\%$), which is why a terminal alkyne C–H is far more acidic than an alkane C–H — a direct, measurable consequence of the hybridization model.

### Where it connects
Hybridization is the orbital-level partner of **VSEPR**: VSEPR gives the shape, hybridization names the orbitals. The $\sigma/\pi$ split underlies **isomerism** (restricted rotation about double bonds) and reactivity in **organic reaction types**.

### Watch out
Hybridization follows from geometry, not the other way around — first count domains (VSEPR), then assign the matching hybridization ($4\to sp^3$, $3\to sp^2$, $2\to sp$). It is a model, so don't treat hybrids as literally "real" orbitals the atom physically forms.

Hybridize the *central* atom to match its geometry, and remember a multiple bond's extra $\pi$ components come from *unhybridized* $p$ orbitals, not from the hybrids — the hybrids only build the $\sigma$ framework.

depths.eli5: An atom's basic electron 'rooms' (orbitals) come in different shapes and don't all point the right way for bonding. So the atom blends them into a fresh set of identical, evenly-spaced rooms that aim straight at its neighbors. With matching rooms pointing the right directions, the bonds all come out the same and the molecule gets a clean symmetric shape.
depths.core: Hybridization describes how an atom mixes its basic atomic orbitals into a new set of equivalent 'hybrid' orbitals aimed at its bonding partners. Example: in methane (CH₄), carbon mixes its one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals into four identical sp³ hybrids that point to the corners of a tetrahedron, giving four equal C–H bonds. Mixing the s with only two p orbitals gives three sp² hybrids in a flat triangle (trigonal planar), leaving one unmixed p orbital available to form a second, side-by-side bond called a π bond. Mixing s with one p gives two sp hybrids in a straight line, leaving two unmixed p orbitals. So hybridization is the orbital-level partner of VSEPR: VSEPR predicts the shape, hybridization names the orbitals that produce it. (A normal end-to-end single bond is called a σ bond.)
depths.deep: Hybridization is a mathematical change of description, not a physical event the atom 'does' — it is the combination of atomic orbitals that best matches the molecule's symmetry, and it conveniently splits the bonding into a σ framework (from the hybrids) and a π system (from leftover unmixed p orbitals). It is descriptive rather than predictive: experiments like photoelectron spectroscopy show the underlying orbitals are not literally all identical, so hybridization is best treated as a useful model.

atoms.title: Molecular orbital theory
atoms.summary: Atomic orbitals combine into delocalized bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals filled by all the molecule's electrons.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Here is a more powerful picture of bonding. When atoms join, their separate orbitals merge into new orbitals belonging to the *whole* molecule. Some pile electron density into the gap between nuclei and act like glue (bonding); others put electrons where they push the atoms apart (antibonding). Whether a molecule holds together depends on which kind the electrons fill.

### Precisely
**Molecular orbital (MO) theory** treats electrons as belonging to the whole molecule. Combining $N$ atomic orbitals yields $N$ molecular orbitals: **in-phase** combinations are **bonding** (lower energy, density between nuclei); **out-of-phase** combinations are **antibonding** (higher energy, a node between nuclei). Fill them lowest-first. The net bonding is the
$$\text{bond order} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,(n_b - n_a),$$
where $n_b$ and $n_a$ are bonding and antibonding electrons.

### Worked example
**Why does $\mathrm{He_2}$ not form?** Each He contributes two $1s$ electrons, $4$ total. They fill the bonding $\sigma_{1s}$ ($2\,e^-$) and the antibonding $\sigma^*_{1s}$ ($2\,e^-$). Bond order $= \tfrac{1}{2}(2-2) = 0$ — no net bond, so $\mathrm{He_2}$ does not exist as a stable molecule. Contrast $\mathrm{H_2}$: only $2$ electrons fill $\sigma_{1s}$, giving bond order $1$.

For $\mathrm{O_2}$ the MO diagram predicts a bond order of $\tfrac{1}{2}(8-4)=2$ *and* two unpaired electrons in the degenerate $\pi^*$ orbitals — so liquid oxygen is genuinely attracted to a magnet, a result you can demonstrate by pouring it between the poles of a magnet and watching it cling.

### Why it's true / how it works
MO theory is the **LCAO** (linear combination of atomic orbitals) approximation to the molecular Schrödinger equation. Filling MOs by the Aufbau principle predicts spectra and magnetism. Its triumph is $\mathrm{O_2}$: its two highest electrons land in a degenerate pair of antibonding $\pi^*$ orbitals with **parallel spins** (Hund's rule), giving two unpaired electrons — so $\mathrm{O_2}$ is **paramagnetic**, a fact Lewis structures get wrong.

The energy ordering of MOs isn't fixed: for the lighter second-row diatomics (up to $\mathrm{N_2}$) the $\sigma_{2p}$ sits *above* the $\pi_{2p}$ because of $s$–$p$ mixing, while for $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $\mathrm{F_2}$ the order flips — a detail that correctly predicts their differing magnetic behavior.

### Where it connects
MO theory explains fractional bond orders, paramagnetism, and the band structure behind **metallic bonding** and semiconductors. It generalises **covalent bonding** and rests on **quantum numbers**.

It also scales upward: the same in-phase/out-of-phase combination logic, applied to an entire crystal of atoms, produces the continuous energy bands of solids — making MO theory the conceptual bridge from a single bond to the band structure that distinguishes metals, semiconductors, and insulators.

### Watch out
An antibonding orbital is a real, occupiable orbital, not "no orbital" — filling it *subtracts* from bonding. And bonding electrons alone don't decide stability; you must subtract the antibonding electrons to get the true bond order.

MO and valence-bond (Lewis/hybridization) pictures are complementary, not contradictory — use Lewis for quick connectivity and geometry, but reach for MO theory whenever magnetism, spectra, or fractional bond orders are involved.

Some of these new rooms hold electrons in the gap between atoms and act like glue (bonding); others put electrons where they actually push the atoms apart (antibonding). Whether a molecule holds together depends on which kind the electrons fill.
depths.core: Molecular orbital (MO) theory treats a molecule's electrons as belonging to the whole molecule, not to individual atoms. When you combine N atomic orbitals you get N molecular orbitals. The 'in-phase' combinations are bonding orbitals — lower energy, with electron density piled between the nuclei (stabilizing). The 'out-of-phase' combinations are antibonding orbitals — higher energy, with a node (a gap of zero electron density) between the nuclei (destabilizing). The net bonding is captured by the bond order = ½ (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons). MO theory explains things the simpler Lewis-dot picture cannot: why oxygen (O₂) is paramagnetic (weakly attracted to a magnet because it has unpaired electrons), why some molecules have fractional bond orders, and why a helium molecule (He₂) never forms.
depths.deep: MO theory is the 'linear combination of atomic orbitals' (LCAO) approximation to the molecular Schrödinger equation. You fill the molecular orbitals from lowest energy up — Aufbau again — which directly predicts spectra and magnetism. For O₂, the two highest electrons land in a pair of equal-energy antibonding (π*) orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule), giving two unpaired electrons and hence its magnetic behavior, a result Lewis structures get wrong.

atoms.title: Metallic bonding
atoms.summary: Metal atoms pool their valence electrons into a delocalized sea (or bands) shared across the whole lattice.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Metals like copper and iron bind a third way. Their outer electrons don't belong to any single atom — they all let go and roam freely through the whole chunk of metal, like a shared swimming pool of electrons sloshing around fixed positive cores. Because the electrons move anywhere, metals carry current; because nothing locks the cores rigidly, you can bend and hammer metal without shattering it.

### Precisely
In **metallic bonding**, each metal atom releases its **valence** electrons into a collective, delocalised pool — the **"electron sea"** — flowing around a lattice of positive **cations**. This explains metals' signature properties: high electrical and thermal **conductivity** (mobile electrons carry charge and energy), **malleability and ductility** (cores slide past one another without snapping a directional bond), and metallic **lustre** (free electrons reflect light).

### Worked example
Take **sodium** metal. Each Na atom donates its single $3s^1$ electron to the shared pool, leaving a lattice of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ cores bathed in mobile electrons. Apply a voltage and the electrons drift, producing current. Strike the metal and the cores shift position, but the non-directional electron sea simply re-accommodates them — so sodium deforms rather than cracking, unlike brittle ionic $\mathrm{NaCl}$.

The model also explains *trends*: magnesium, donating two valence electrons per atom into the sea, is harder and higher-melting than sodium, which donates only one — more pooled electrons and higher core charges mean stronger metallic bonding overall.

### Why it's true / how it works
The electron-sea picture is the simple limit of **band theory**: when many atomic orbitals overlap across a huge number of atoms, their levels merge into continuous **bands**. Conduction occurs when a band is only partly filled, leaving nearby empty states for electrons to move into. The gap (if any) between the filled valence band and empty conduction band distinguishes **metals** (no gap), **semiconductors** (small gap), and **insulators** (large gap).

In band language, sodium's half-filled $3s$-derived band leaves abundant empty states just above the filled ones, so an applied field accelerates electrons freely — that partial filling, not merely the presence of electrons, is the precise condition for metallic conduction.

### Where it connects
Metallic bonding completes the trio with **ionic** and **covalent** bonding, and its delocalisation is a macroscopic cousin of **molecular orbital theory**. Band theory connects onward to electronics and **coordination complexes**.

### Watch out
The "sea" is not a chaotic gas of unbound electrons — they are still confined to the metal and obey quantum (band) structure. And conductivity actually *decreases* as a metal heats up, because lattice vibrations scatter the moving electrons more.

Beware treating the electron sea as totally free: real metals show quantum band structure, and alloying or impurities scatter the carriers, which is why pure metals conduct better than their alloys and why semiconductors (small band gap) behave so differently.

Because the electrons are delocalized (not tied to one atom), this picture explains the signature properties of metals: they conduct electricity and heat well (the free electrons carry charge and energy), they are malleable and ductile (you can bend or stretch them because the cores slide past each other without snapping any directional bond), and they have a shiny metallic luster (the free electrons reflect light).

atoms.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
atoms.summary: A mole is a fixed count of particles that links the atomic scale to gram-scale laboratory amounts.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Atoms are so tiny that even a pinch of matter holds mind-bending numbers of them — far too many to count one by one. So chemists invented a counting word for a fixed, huge batch: the **mole**. Just as "a dozen" always means $12$, "a mole" always means about $6.022\times10^{23}$. With a counting word this large, you can weigh out a known number of atoms on an ordinary balance.

### Precisely
A **mole** is a fixed count of particles equal to **Avogadro's number**:
$$N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}.$$
The **molar mass** of a substance — the mass of one mole, in $\text{g/mol}$ — is numerically equal to its average atomic or molecular mass (the periodic-table value). The link between mass, moles, and count is
$$n = \frac{m}{M}, \qquad N = n\,N_A.$$

### Worked example
How many molecules are in $18\ \text{g}$ of water? The molar mass of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is $2(1.008) + 16.00 \approx 18.0\ \text{g/mol}$. So $n = 18\ \text{g} \div 18\ \text{g/mol} = 1\ \text{mol}$, and the number of molecules is $N = 1 \times 6.022\times10^{23} = 6.022\times10^{23}$.

Going the other way: how much does $3.011\times10^{23}$ atoms of carbon weigh? That is $0.5\ \text{mol}$ (half of $N_A$), and carbon's molar mass is $12.01\ \text{g/mol}$, so the mass is $0.5 \times 12.01 \approx 6.0\ \text{g}$.

### Why it's true / how it works
The mole works because molar mass is *defined* to make one mole of a substance weigh, in grams, what one particle weighs in atomic mass units. Since the 2019 SI redefinition, $N_A$ is an **exact, defined** constant, so the mole is now simply that fixed particle count rather than something measured. Atomic masses remain weighted averages over an element's naturally occurring **isotopes**.

The whole scheme hangs together because $1\ \text{u}$ (the atomic-scale mass unit) times $N_A$ equals exactly $1\ \text{g/mol}$ — that single numerical coincidence, built into the definitions, is what lets a periodic-table mass in "u" double as a molar mass in "g/mol."

### Where it connects
The mole is the gateway to **stoichiometry**, the $n$ in the **ideal gas law** $PV=nRT$, and the concentration unit (molarity) in **solutions**. It bridges the atomic and gram scales.

Practically, the mole is the unit you will use in almost every later calculation — balancing equations, finding limiting reagents, computing concentrations, and applying the gas laws — so fluency in converting between mass, moles, and number of particles pays off on every problem that follows.

### Watch out
A mole counts *particles*, but you must specify *which* — atoms, molecules, ions, or electrons. One mole of $\mathrm{O_2}$ contains $6.022\times10^{23}$ molecules but $2\times$ that many oxygen atoms.

Avogadro's number is enormous but it is *just a count* — a mole of marbles would bury the Earth, yet a mole of atoms fits in a spoonful, because atoms are unimaginably small. Don't let the size of $N_A$ obscure that it plays the same role as "dozen."

With a counting word this size, you can weigh out a known number of atoms on a scale.

So one mole of carbon weighs about 12 grams; one mole of water weighs about 18 grams. This lets a chemist weigh a sample and immediately know how many particles it holds — the foundation of doing chemistry by the numbers.

atoms.title: Stoichiometry and balanced equations
atoms.summary: Balanced chemical equations fix the mole ratios that convert amounts of reactants into amounts of products.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A chemical reaction is a recipe written in symbols. A **balanced equation** is a recipe where the ingredients (reactants) on the left turn into results (products) on the right, with the numbers worked out so every atom is accounted for — nothing is created or destroyed, only rearranged. The numbers in front tell you exactly how much of each ingredient you need.

### Precisely
**Stoichiometry** is the quantitative relationship between amounts of reactants and products. A **balanced equation** has equal counts of each element on both sides, enforcing **conservation of mass**. The coefficients are **mole ratios** that act as conversion factors. Key ideas: the **limiting reagent** (runs out first, caps the product), the **theoretical yield**, and the **percent yield** $= (\text{actual}/\text{theoretical})\times 100\%$.

### Worked example
Burn hydrogen: $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}$. Suppose you have $3\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{H_2}$ and $3\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{O_2}$. The ratio needs $\mathrm{H_2}:\mathrm{O_2} = 2:1$, so $3\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{H_2}$ requires only $1.5\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{O_2}$. Since $1.5 < 3$, hydrogen runs out first — **$\mathrm{H_2}$ is limiting**. It produces $3\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{H_2O}$, leaving $3 - 1.5 = 1.5\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{O_2}$ in excess.

Continuing, if the $3\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{H_2}$ above actually produced only $2.4\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{H_2O}$ instead of the theoretical $3\ \text{mol}$, the **percent yield** is $(2.4/3.0)\times100\% = 80\%$ — the kind of efficiency figure that governs the economics of any industrial process.

### Why it's true / how it works
Stoichiometry is bookkeeping forced by the **conservation of atoms** (and, for ions, of charge). Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so each element's count must match on both sides — that is exactly what balancing enforces. For redox reactions you must also balance the **electrons** transferred.

Balancing is really solving a small system of conservation equations — one per element — for the coefficients, which is why complex equations can be balanced systematically (or by algebra) rather than by trial and error alone. For ionic and redox equations, charge is conserved too, adding one more equation to the set.

### Where it connects
Stoichiometry builds on the **mole concept** and feeds into **thermochemistry** (heats of reaction), **gas-law** volume calculations, **titration**, and equilibrium. It is the arithmetic backbone of all quantitative chemistry.

Because every quantitative result in chemistry — yields, concentrations, gas volumes, heats of reaction, electron counts in electrochemistry — flows through mole ratios, stoichiometry is less a single topic than the connective tissue linking nearly every chapter that comes after it.

### Watch out
Coefficients are *mole* ratios, not mass ratios — you cannot compare grams directly; convert to moles first. And the limiting reagent is set by comparing moles **relative to coefficients**, not by which reactant has fewer raw moles.

A subtle trap: never "balance" by changing a chemical *subscript* (that would change the substance, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ into $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$); only the coefficients out front may be adjusted.

Those coefficients are mole ratios: they tell you the proportions in which substances combine, and act as conversion factors between any two substances in the reaction. With them you can predict how much product forms, find the limiting reagent (the ingredient that runs out first and caps the amount of product), and compute the percent yield (how much you actually got versus the theoretical maximum).

For redox reactions — where electrons move — you must also balance the electrons transferred. The limiting reagent is whichever runs out first relative to its coefficient; it alone sets the theoretical yield, and whatever is left over is the 'excess' reagent.

atoms.title: The ideal gas law
atoms.summary: Pressure, volume, amount, and temperature of a dilute gas obey one combined relation.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Gases respond to squeezing and heating in simple ways: squeeze a gas into a smaller space and its pressure climbs; warm it and it pushes harder or expands. One neat formula ties pressure, volume, amount, and temperature together at once — a remarkably good description of any dilute gas.

### Precisely
$$PV = nRT$$
where $P$ is pressure, $V$ volume, $n$ moles, $T$ the **absolute** temperature (in kelvin), and $R$ the gas constant:
$$R = 8.314\ \text{J·mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = 0.08206\ \text{L·atm·mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}.$$
It bundles **Boyle's law** ($P \propto 1/V$ at fixed $n,T$), **Charles's law** ($V \propto T$), and **Avogadro's law** ($V \propto n$). It models molecules as non-interacting points — accurate at low pressure and high temperature.

### Worked example
A $2.0\ \text{L}$ vessel holds $0.50\ \text{mol}$ of gas at $300\ \text{K}$. The pressure is
$$P = \frac{nRT}{V} = \frac{(0.50)(0.08206)(300)}{2.0} \approx 6.2\ \text{atm}.$$
Now halve the volume to $1.0\ \text{L}$ at fixed $n$ and $T$: $P$ doubles to about $12.3\ \text{atm}$, the Boyle's-law result $P \propto 1/V$.

For a temperature change at fixed $n$ and $V$, the law gives $P/T = \text{const}$, so heating that $1.0\ \text{L}$ sample from $300\ \text{K}$ to $600\ \text{K}$ doubles its pressure again — pressure rises in direct proportion to absolute temperature, the content of Gay-Lussac's law.

### Why it's true / how it works
$PV=nRT$ follows from **kinetic-molecular theory**: pressure is the cumulative push of molecules striking the walls, and absolute temperature measures their average kinetic energy. Real gases deviate when molecules are crowded enough that their finite size and mutual attractions matter; the **van der Waals equation** $\left(P + a\,n^2/V^2\right)(V - nb) = nRT$ patches in both corrections.

A useful corollary is the molar volume: at standard temperature and pressure ($273\ \text{K}$, $1\ \text{atm}$) one mole of any ideal gas occupies about $22.4\ \text{L}$ — a direct consequence of $V = nRT/P$ and a fast way to convert gas volumes to moles in stoichiometry problems.

### Where it connects
The law rests on the **mole concept** and leads into **kinetic-molecular theory**, gas **stoichiometry**, and **partial-pressure** equilibria. The constant $R$ reappears throughout thermodynamics.

The same law also underlies partial pressures in gas-phase equilibria and the molar-volume conversions used in reaction stoichiometry, so $PV=nRT$ reappears far beyond the gases chapter as a routine tool throughout physical chemistry.

### Watch out
$T$ must be in **kelvin** — using Celsius gives nonsense (and divides by zero or negatives). Watch units on $R$: match it to your pressure unit (atm vs. Pa) and volume unit (L vs. m³).

The ideal law also fails near condensation — at high pressure or low temperature, where attractions pull molecules together and the gas is about to liquefy, real behavior departs sharply from $PV=nRT$ and you need the van der Waals correction.

One neat formula, PV = nRT, ties together pressure (P), volume (V), the amount of gas (n), and temperature (T) all at once.

R is a fixed number called the gas constant. The law bundles three older observations: at fixed amount, pressure and volume are inversely related (Boyle's law — squeeze to half the volume, double the pressure); volume grows with temperature (Charles's law); and equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules at the same P and T (Avogadro's law). It pictures gas molecules as tiny points that don't attract each other — a very good approximation when the gas is dilute (low pressure, high temperature).

Real gases deviate from the ideal law when molecules are crowded enough that their own size and their mutual attractions matter; the van der Waals equation, (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, patches in corrections for both effects.
