atoms.title: Kinetic-molecular theory
atoms.summary: Gas behavior follows from many tiny particles in constant random motion whose average kinetic energy is set by temperature.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Zoom in on a gas and it is a vast swarm of tiny balls zooming in all directions and bouncing off the container walls. The constant drumming of those bounces is what we feel as **pressure**, and how fast the balls move on average is what we measure as **temperature**. Hotter means faster.

### Precisely
**Kinetic-molecular theory** derives the gas laws from a model of countless tiny molecules in constant random motion, assuming: molecules are small compared to their separations, they exert no long-range attractions, and collisions are **elastic** (no energy lost). Two results follow: pressure is the molecules' collective force on the walls, and absolute temperature is proportional to their average kinetic energy,
$$\tfrac{1}{2}m\langle v^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_B T.$$
Molecular speeds spread out as the **Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution**.

### Worked example
At the same temperature, do **helium** or **oxygen** molecules move faster? Both have the same average kinetic energy $\tfrac{3}{2}k_B T$, so $\tfrac{1}{2}m\langle v^2\rangle$ is equal, giving $\langle v^2\rangle \propto 1/m$. Helium ($M \approx 4$) is far lighter than $\mathrm{O_2}$ ($M \approx 32$), so $\langle v^2 \rangle_{\text{He}}/\langle v^2 \rangle_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 32/4 = 8$ and helium's typical speed is $\sqrt{8}\approx 2.8\times$ larger.

This directly predicts **Graham's law**: helium ($M\approx 4$) effuses through a pinhole $\sqrt{32/4}=\sqrt{8}\approx 2.8$ times faster than oxygen ($M\approx 32$), because effusion rate scales as $1/\sqrt{M}$ — the same square-root-of-mass dependence as the speeds.

### Why it's true / how it works
Average speed scales as $\sqrt{T/M}$, so light molecules move faster at a given $T$. This explains **effusion** rates (Graham's law: leakage through a tiny hole $\propto 1/\sqrt{M}$) and why light hydrogen escapes a planet's gravity while heavier $\mathrm{CO_2}$ stays. The high-speed **tail** of the distribution — the small fraction of unusually energetic molecules — is exactly what drives reaction rates.

The factor of $\tfrac{3}{2}$ in $\tfrac{1}{2}m\langle v^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$ comes from the three independent directions of motion (x, y, z), each contributing $\tfrac{1}{2}k_BT$ — an instance of the equipartition principle, which assigns that much energy to every quadratic degree of freedom.

### Where it connects
This theory is the microscopic foundation of the **ideal gas law**, and its energetic tail underlies the **Arrhenius** picture of reaction rates. The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ links to entropy.

Its deepest payoff is conceptual unification: pressure, temperature, diffusion, effusion, and even the energetic threshold for reactions all turn out to be different views of the same underlying molecular motion, which is why this theory is the hinge between the macroscopic gas laws and microscopic kinetics.

### Watch out
Temperature reflects *average* kinetic energy, not the speed of any one molecule — at any instant some move much faster, some barely at all. And it is the **distribution's tail**, not the average, that controls how fast reactions go.

Temperature reflects only *translational* (motion-through-space) kinetic energy in this simple picture; real molecules also store energy in rotation and vibration, which is why polyatomic gases have larger heat capacities than monatomic ones.

depths.eli5: Zoom in on a gas and it's a huge swarm of tiny balls (the molecules) zooming around in all directions and bouncing off the walls of their container. The constant drumming of these bounces is what we feel as pressure, and how fast the balls zoom on average is what we measure as temperature. Hotter = faster.
depths.core: Kinetic-molecular theory explains where the gas laws come from by modeling a gas as countless tiny molecules in constant, random motion. The assumptions: the molecules are very small compared to the space between them, they don't attract each other, and their collisions are 'elastic' (no energy lost). From these, two key ideas follow: pressure is the combined force of molecules hammering the container walls, and absolute temperature is directly proportional to the molecules' average kinetic energy of motion. The molecules don't all move at one speed — their speeds are spread out in a predictable pattern called the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.
depths.deep: The central result is ½m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT (average kinetic energy is set by temperature, where k_B is the Boltzmann constant). This means average speed scales as the square root of T/M, so lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature. That explains effusion rates (how fast a gas leaks through a tiny hole — Graham's law) and why light hydrogen escapes a planet's gravity while heavier CO₂ stays. The high-speed 'tail' of the distribution — the small fraction of unusually fast, energetic molecules — is exactly what drives the rates of chemical reactions.

quiz.answer: The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules.

atoms.title: Intermolecular forces
atoms.summary: Attractions between whole molecules — dispersion, dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding — set boiling points and phase behavior.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Strong bonds hold the atoms *inside* a molecule together, but much weaker forces act *between* whole, separate molecules. Even neutral molecules feel a faint stickiness toward their neighbours. The stickier the molecules, the more energy it takes to pull them apart — so the higher the boiling point.

### Precisely
**Intermolecular forces (IMFs)** are attractions between molecules, weaker than covalent bonds, in three main kinds (weakest to strongest):

- **London dispersion** — present in *all* molecules; momentary uneven electron distributions create fleeting dipoles. Strength grows with molecular size (polarisability).
- **Dipole–dipole** — between permanently polar molecules, which align $+$ to $-$.
- **Hydrogen bonding** — strongest; an H bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby N, O, or F.

These set boiling point, viscosity, and surface tension.

### Worked example
Why does **water** boil at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ while methane ($\mathrm{CH_4}$, similar molar mass) boils at $-162\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Methane is nonpolar, so only weak dispersion forces hold its molecules. Water's $\mathrm{O{-}H}$ bonds let each molecule form multiple **hydrogen bonds** to neighbours. Breaking that extensive network to vaporise water demands far more energy, lifting its boiling point roughly $160\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ above what its mass alone would predict.

Within a family the trend is clean: the boiling points of the noble gases climb He $<$ Ne $<$ Ar $<$ Kr $<$ Xe, purely because larger atoms are more polarizable and so have stronger **dispersion** forces — no permanent dipoles or hydrogen bonds involved at all.

### Why it's true / how it works
All three forces are ultimately electrostatic but differ in range. Dispersion arises from correlated quantum fluctuations of electron clouds and falls off steeply, as $r^{-6}$. Hydrogen bonding is strong because the small, exposed H$^{\delta+}$ approaches a concentrated lone pair very closely. This network is why liquid water is structured, how proteins fold, and how DNA's two strands pair.

Hydrogen bonding's special strength comes from two things at once: the very large $\mathrm{H}$–to–$\mathrm{N/O/F}$ electronegativity gap creates a strongly $\delta+$ hydrogen, and that bare, tiny hydrogen can approach the partner's lone pair far more closely than any other atom could — concentrating the electrostatic attraction.

### Where it connects
IMFs follow from **electronegativity and polarity**, govern **states of matter** and phase transitions, drive **solubility** ("like dissolves like"), and explain **colligative** behaviour.

### Watch out
A hydrogen *bond* is an intermolecular attraction, not a covalent bond, and it requires H bonded specifically to **N, O, or F** — not to carbon. Don't confuse the strong intramolecular bonds with the weak forces *between* molecules; boiling breaks the latter, not the former.

Don't rank forces by type alone while ignoring size: a large nonpolar molecule can out-stick a small polar one because cumulative dispersion forces grow with surface area — which is why long-chain hydrocarbons are waxy solids despite being nonpolar.

depths.eli5: There are strong forces holding the atoms inside a molecule together — but there are also much weaker forces of attraction between whole, separate molecules. Even molecules with no overall charge feel a faint stickiness toward their neighbors. The stickier the molecules, the more energy it takes to pull them apart, so the higher the boiling point.
depths.core: Intermolecular forces are the attractions between separate molecules (as opposed to the bonds inside a molecule). There are three main kinds, from weakest to strongest. London dispersion forces exist between all molecules: at any instant an electron cloud can be lopsided, creating a fleeting tiny dipole (a plus end and a minus end) that pulls on a neighbor; these grow stronger as molecules get bigger. Dipole-dipole forces act between permanently polar molecules (ones with a fixed plus and minus end), which line up plus-to-minus. Hydrogen bonding is the strongest: it occurs when a hydrogen atom bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby N, O, or F. Together these forces set boiling points, viscosity (thickness), and surface tension.
depths.deep: All three are ultimately electrostatic, but differ in range and strength; dispersion comes from correlated quantum fluctuations of electron clouds and falls off as r⁻⁶ (very fast with distance). Hydrogen bonding is why water boils about 160 °C higher than its small mass would predict, and it is the organizing force behind liquid water's structure, how proteins fold into shape, and how the two strands of DNA pair up.

quiz.answer: London dispersion forces (induced-dipole / induced-dipole).

atoms.title: States of matter and phase transitions
atoms.summary: Solid, liquid, and gas reflect the contest between intermolecular attraction and thermal motion, mapped by a phase diagram.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Water can be ice, liquid, or steam — same molecules, just different amounts of energy. Cold molecules barely move and lock into a rigid solid; warm them and they loosen into a flowing liquid; heat them more and they break free as a gas. It's a tug-of-war between the molecules' stickiness, which holds them together, and their thermal energy, which flings them apart.

### Precisely
The three common **states of matter** — solid, liquid, gas — reflect a contest between **intermolecular attraction** and **thermal energy** (which rises with temperature $T$). A **phase diagram** maps which state is stable at each pressure and temperature, with lines marking transitions. Two special points appear: the **triple point** (solid, liquid, gas all coexist) and the **critical point** (beyond which liquid and gas merge into one indistinguishable phase).

### Worked example
Trace heating ice at $1\ \text{atm}$ on water's phase diagram. Start as solid at $-20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; cross the solid–liquid line at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (melting); cross the liquid–gas line at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (boiling). Water's triple point sits at $0.01\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $0.006\ \text{atm}$; its critical point at $374\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $218\ \text{atm}$. Above that critical point, no amount of pressure will condense steam into a distinct liquid.

**Carbon dioxide** illustrates the triple point's importance: at $1\ \text{atm}$ its solid ("dry ice") never melts but **sublimes** straight to gas, because its triple-point pressure ($5.1\ \text{atm}$) lies *above* atmospheric — so a liquid phase only exists under pressure.

### Why it's true / how it works
A phase transition occurs where the molar **Gibbs free energies** of two phases become equal — at that boundary neither is more stable, so they coexist. The **Clausius–Clapeyron relation** gives the slope of the liquid–gas line. Past the critical point the distinction vanishes into a **supercritical fluid**, used as a green solvent (e.g. supercritical $\mathrm{CO_2}$ to decaffeinate coffee).

Each transition has a latent heat (fusion, vaporization, sublimation) absorbed or released at constant temperature, because the energy goes entirely into rearranging intermolecular bonds rather than raising the temperature — which is why a pot of boiling water holds at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ until it has all vaporized.

### Where it connects
States of matter rest on **intermolecular forces** and **kinetic-molecular theory**, and the boundaries are governed by **Gibbs free energy** and the **Clausius–Clapeyron** equation.

The same attraction-versus-thermal-energy contest reappears in solubility, surface tension, and viscosity, so the phase-diagram picture is really a special case of a broader theme: matter's behavior is set everywhere by the balance between forces pulling molecules together and heat driving them apart.

### Watch out
Water's solid–liquid line slopes *backward* (negative slope) — ice is less dense than liquid water, so higher pressure can *melt* ice. Most substances behave the opposite way, so don't generalise water's quirk.

Beyond the critical point there is no boiling and no meniscus — the supercritical fluid is neither liquid nor gas, so don't expect a phase boundary to cross when you heat a fluid past that point.

depths.eli5: Water can be ice, liquid, or steam — same molecules, just different amounts of energy. When molecules are cold they barely move and lock into a rigid solid; warm them and they loosen into a flowing liquid; heat them more and they break free entirely as a gas. It's a tug-of-war between the molecules' stickiness (which wants to hold them together) and their heat energy (which wants to fling them apart).
depths.core: The three common states of matter — solid, liquid, and gas — reflect a contest between intermolecular attraction (the stickiness holding molecules together) and thermal energy (random motion, which increases with temperature T). When stickiness wins you get a solid; as heat wins out you progress to liquid then gas. A phase diagram is a map that shows which state is stable at any given pressure and temperature, with lines marking where transitions happen. Two special spots appear on it: the triple point, the unique pressure and temperature where solid, liquid, and gas all coexist; and the critical point, beyond which the liquid and gas blur into one and can no longer be told apart.
depths.deep: A phase transition occurs where the 'free energy' (a stability measure) of two phases becomes equal; at that boundary the molar Gibbs energies of the two phases match. The Clausius–Clapeyron relation gives the slope of the liquid–gas (vapor-pressure) line on the diagram. Past the critical point the liquid/gas distinction vanishes into a supercritical fluid — a state with in-between properties that's used as an environmentally friendly 'green' solvent, for example to decaffeinate coffee with supercritical CO₂.

quiz.answer: The unique pressure and temperature where solid, liquid, and gas phases all coexist in equilibrium.

quiz.answer: Adding thermal energy increases molecular motion until it overcomes the intermolecular attractions holding molecules in fixed (solid) then close (liquid) arrangements, finally freeing them as a gas.

atoms.title: Solutions and concentration
atoms.summary: A solute dissolves in a solvent when their intermolecular interactions are compatible, with concentration measured in molarity.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Stir sugar into water and it vanishes — that is dissolving, forming a **solution**. The thing that dissolves (sugar) is the **solute**; the liquid it dissolves into (water) is the **solvent**. Things dissolve when they "get along" with the liquid: salt and sugar love water, oil refuses to mix. **Concentration** simply measures how crowded the dissolved stuff is.

### Precisely
A **solution** is a homogeneous mixture of a **solute** in a **solvent**. Solubility follows **"like dissolves like"**: polar and ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents; nonpolar solutes in nonpolar solvents. Dissolving trades solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions for new solute–solvent ones. The most common concentration unit is **molarity**:
$$M = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{litres of solution}}\ (\text{mol/L}).$$

### Worked example
How many moles of solute are in $250\ \text{mL}$ of a $0.40\ \text{M}$ solution? Convert volume to litres: $250\ \text{mL} = 0.250\ \text{L}$. Then
$$n = M \times V = 0.40\ \text{mol/L} \times 0.250\ \text{L} = 0.10\ \text{mol}.$$
To prepare it, you would dissolve $0.10\ \text{mol}$ of solute and add solvent up to a *total* volume of $250\ \text{mL}$.

Dilution is the everyday companion calculation: to make the $0.40\ \text{M}$ solution from a $2.0\ \text{M}$ stock, use $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$, so $V_1 = (0.40)(0.250)/2.0 = 0.050\ \text{L}$ — measure $50\ \text{mL}$ of stock and dilute to $250\ \text{mL}$.

### Why it's true / how it works
Whether a substance dissolves depends on the **Gibbs free energy of mixing**, usually helped by a large favourable **entropy** of mixing. For an ionic solid it is a close contest between **lattice energy** (the cost of breaking the crystal) and **hydration energy** (the payoff as water surrounds the freed ions). Once dissolved, solutes produce **colligative properties** that depend only on particle count.

Solubility itself is temperature-dependent and not always intuitive: most solids dissolve better in hot water (dissolving is usually endothermic for them), but most **gases** dissolve *worse* as temperature rises, which is why a warm soda goes flat and why thermal pollution lowers a river's dissolved oxygen.

### Where it connects
Solutions build on **intermolecular forces** and the **mole concept**, feed **stoichiometry** in solution, **titration**, and aqueous **equilibria** (acids, bases, buffers), and lead to **colligative properties**.

Solutions are also the stage on which most of the rest of chemistry is performed — acids and bases, buffers, titrations, equilibria, and electrochemistry nearly all happen in aqueous solution — so molarity is the concentration unit you will reach for again and again.

### Watch out
Molarity is moles per litre of **solution**, not of solvent — add solvent *to* the final volume, don't add a litre *of* solvent. And molarity changes with temperature (volume expands), unlike molality.

"Like dissolves like" is a guideline, not a guarantee — and it is about the *whole molecule's* polarity: a long nonpolar tail can make an otherwise polar molecule (like a fatty alcohol) refuse to dissolve in water.

depths.eli5: When you stir sugar into water and it disappears, that's dissolving — a solution. The thing that dissolves (sugar) is the solute; the liquid it dissolves into (water) is the solvent. Things dissolve when they 'get along' with the liquid: salt and sugar love water, but oil refuses to mix with it. 'Concentration' is just a way of saying how crowded the dissolved stuff is.
depths.core: A solution is a uniform mixture of a solute (the dissolved substance) in a solvent (the dissolving liquid). Whether something dissolves follows the rule 'like dissolves like': polar and ionic solutes (with charged or lopsided molecules) dissolve in polar solvents like water, while nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents like oil. Dissolving means trading the attractions among solute particles and among solvent particles for new attractions between solute and solvent. Concentration is most often given as molarity — moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L) — a number that plugs directly into stoichiometry and equilibrium calculations.
depths.deep: Whether a substance dissolves depends on the Gibbs free energy of mixing, which usually has a large favorable entropy (disorder) term pushing things to mix. For an ionic solid, dissolving is a close contest between the lattice energy holding the crystal together (a cost) and the hydration energy released when water surrounds the freed ions (a payoff). Once dissolved, the solute produces colligative properties — boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, and osmotic pressure — that depend only on how many dissolved particles there are, not what they are.

atoms.title: Enthalpy and heats of reaction
atoms.summary: Enthalpy change is the heat exchanged at constant pressure, negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Reactions move heat around. Some give off heat — the beaker warms, like a hand-warmer. Others soak it up and go cold, like an instant cold-pack. **Enthalpy** is the accounting word for that heat. A reaction's enthalpy change tells you how much heat it released or absorbed.

### Precisely
**Enthalpy** $H$ measures heat content; what matters is the **enthalpy change** $\Delta H$. At constant pressure (normal open-lab conditions),
$$\Delta H = q_p,$$
the heat exchanged. **Exothermic** reactions release heat, $\Delta H < 0$; **endothermic** reactions absorb it, $\Delta H > 0$. Because $H$ is a **state function** (path-independent), **Hess's law** lets you add step enthalpies, and
$$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \sum \Delta H^\circ_f(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H^\circ_f(\text{reactants}).$$

### Worked example
For the combustion of methane,
$$\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l)},$$
use standard formation enthalpies (kJ/mol): $\mathrm{CH_4}\,-74.8$, $\mathrm{CO_2}\,-393.5$, $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\,-285.8$, and $\mathrm{O_2}=0$ (an element). Then
$$\Delta H^\circ = [(-393.5) + 2(-285.8)] - [(-74.8) + 0] = -890.3\ \text{kJ/mol}.$$
Strongly negative — combustion is highly exothermic, as expected.

Hess's law lets you reach $\Delta H$ for a reaction you cannot run directly: if you know $\Delta H$ for $\mathrm{C + O_2 \to CO_2}$ and for $\mathrm{CO + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2 \to CO_2}$, subtracting the second from the first gives $\Delta H$ for the hard-to-measure $\mathrm{C + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2 \to CO}$.

### Why it's true / how it works
Formally $H = U + PV$, where $U$ is internal energy; the $PV$ term is why heat at constant pressure ($\Delta H$) differs from heat at constant volume ($\Delta U$) by the expansion work done on the surroundings. Hess's law works precisely because $H$ depends only on initial and final states, so any convenient path gives the same $\Delta H$.

Because enthalpy is a state function, *any* path from reactants to products gives the same $\Delta H$ — so you may invent the most convenient imaginary route (break everything into elements, then rebuild) and the answer is guaranteed correct. This path-independence is what makes tabulated formation enthalpies so powerful.

### Where it connects
Enthalpy builds on **stoichiometry**, pairs with **entropy** in the **Gibbs free energy** spontaneity test, and can be estimated from **bond energies**. The $\mathrm{O{-}H}$ and $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ bonds explain combustion's large $\Delta H$.

Enthalpy is also the entry point to the broader machinery of thermodynamics: paired with entropy it yields the Gibbs free energy that decides spontaneity, and tabulated formation enthalpies make it possible to predict the heat of essentially any reaction from a single reference table.

### Watch out
Mind the **sign**: $\Delta H < 0$ means heat *leaves* the system. And elements in their standard state have $\Delta H^\circ_f = 0$ by definition — a common slip is to look up a nonzero value for $\mathrm{O_2}$ or $\mathrm{N_2}$.

$\Delta H$ tells you the heat, not whether the reaction happens: an endothermic reaction ($\Delta H>0$) can still be spontaneous if entropy rises enough — the full decision belongs to Gibbs free energy, not enthalpy alone.

'Enthalpy' is just the accounting word for tracking that heat. A reaction's enthalpy change tells you how much heat it released or absorbed.
depths.core: Enthalpy (symbol H) is a measure of a substance's heat content. What chemists usually care about is the enthalpy change of a reaction, written ΔH (the Greek delta means 'change in'). At constant pressure — the normal condition in an open lab — ΔH equals the heat the reaction exchanges with its surroundings. A reaction that releases heat is exothermic, and it has ΔH < 0 (negative), which happens because the new bonds in the products are more stable (lower energy) than the bonds in the reactants. A reaction that absorbs heat is endothermic, with ΔH > 0 (positive). Because enthalpy is a state function (it depends only on the start and end, not the route taken), Hess's law lets you add up the enthalpy changes of separate steps to get the overall ΔH.
depths.deep: Formally H = U + PV, where U is internal energy; the PV term is why heat measured at constant pressure (ΔH) differs from heat at constant volume (ΔU) by the work done pushing back the surroundings as the system expands. Chemists tabulate standard enthalpies of formation — the ΔH to make one mole of a compound from its pure elements — and then compute any reaction's enthalpy as ΔH°_rxn = Σ ΔH°_f(products) − Σ ΔH°_f(reactants).

quiz.answer: Negative (ΔH < 0) — heat is released to the surroundings.

quiz.answer: Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not the path — step enthalpies add to the overall value.

atoms.title: Entropy and the second law
atoms.summary: Entropy measures the number of microscopic arrangements, and isolated systems evolve toward higher total entropy.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Entropy measures how many different ways the pieces of a system can be arranged while still looking the same overall. There are vastly more messy, spread-out arrangements than tidy ones, so things naturally drift toward being spread out — which is why a drop of dye disperses through water and never gathers itself back into a drop. Nature tends toward the arrangement that can happen the most ways.

### Precisely
**Entropy** $S$ counts the microscopic arrangements (**microstates**, $W$) consistent with a system's observed state. Boltzmann's relation makes this exact:
$$S = k_B \ln W,$$
with $k_B = 1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}$. The **second law of thermodynamics** states that for any spontaneous process the **total** entropy of the universe (system $+$ surroundings) increases:
$$\Delta S_{\text{univ}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} + \Delta S_{\text{surr}} > 0.$$

### Worked example
A gas initially confined to one half of a box is released. With $N$ molecules, the number of arrangements jumps by a factor of $2^N$ once they can occupy the whole box, so $\Delta S = k_B \ln(2^N) = N k_B \ln 2 > 0$. For a mole, that is $R\ln 2 \approx 5.8\ \text{J/K}$ — positive, so the gas spreads spontaneously and never spontaneously re-crowds into one half.

Phase changes show entropy concretely: melting ice and boiling water both *raise* entropy ($\Delta S > 0$) because molecules gain freedom (solid $\to$ liquid $\to$ gas adds microstates), and indeed vaporization's entropy jump is much larger than melting's, reflecting the gas phase's vastly greater disorder.

### Why it's true / how it works
Entropy is a *count*, not vague "messiness." A reaction can lower the system's own entropy and still be spontaneous if it dumps enough heat to raise the surroundings' entropy more, via
$$\Delta S_{\text{surr}} = -\frac{\Delta H}{T}.$$
Heat released at lower temperature raises entropy most. This trade-off is exactly what **Gibbs free energy** repackages into a system-only test.

The third law of thermodynamics anchors the scale: a perfect crystal at absolute zero has a single accessible arrangement, $W=1$, so $S = k_B\ln 1 = 0$. This zero point lets chemists tabulate *absolute* entropies (unlike enthalpy, which only ever has a reference-relative value).

### Where it connects
Entropy combines with **enthalpy** in **Gibbs free energy**, underlies **colligative properties** and **solution** mixing, and links to the molecular speed spread in **kinetic-molecular theory**.

### Watch out
The second law applies to the **total** (system $+$ surroundings) entropy — a system's entropy *can* fall locally (water freezing, a cell organising) as long as the surroundings gain more. "Entropy always increases" is true only for the universe, not for every subsystem.

Resist equating entropy with sloppy "disorder" — it is a precise microstate count, and counterintuitive cases (some solutions that *order* on mixing, or proteins that fold while total entropy rises) only make sense through the count, not the metaphor.

depths.eli5: Entropy is a measure of how many different ways the bits of something can be arranged while still looking the same overall. There are far more messy, spread-out arrangements than tidy ones, so things naturally drift toward being spread out — that's why a drop of dye disperses through water and never gathers back into a drop on its own. Nature tends toward the arrangement that can happen the most ways.
depths.core: Entropy (symbol S) counts how many microscopic arrangements ('microstates', W) are consistent with what you actually observe. Boltzmann's equation S = k ln W (k is the Boltzmann constant) makes this precise: more possible arrangements means higher entropy. The second law of thermodynamics says that in any spontaneous (self-occurring) process, the total entropy of the universe — the system plus its surroundings — increases. This is why gases expand to fill a room, heat flows from hot to cold, and dissolved substances spread out evenly: each of these moves toward the state that can be realized in vastly more ways.
depths.deep: Entropy is not vaguely 'messiness' — it is a precise count of accessible microstates. A reaction can lower the system's own entropy and still be spontaneous if it releases enough heat to raise the surroundings' entropy by more (ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T, where heat dumped at lower temperature raises entropy most). That trade-off between system and surroundings is exactly what the Gibbs free energy criterion repackages into a convenient system-only test.

quiz.answer: The number of microstates (microscopic arrangements) consistent with the system's macrostate.

atoms.title: Gibbs free energy
atoms.summary: At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous when its Gibbs free energy change is negative.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Wouldn't it be handy to have one number that tells you whether a reaction happens on its own? **Gibbs free energy** is that number. If a reaction's Gibbs energy goes *down* (the change is negative), the reaction is "downhill" and proceeds spontaneously. If it would go up, the reaction won't run unless you push it.

### Precisely
**Gibbs free energy** $G$ bundles enthalpy and entropy into one spontaneity test at constant temperature and pressure:
$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S,$$
with $\Delta H$ the enthalpy change, $\Delta S$ the entropy change, and $T$ the absolute temperature. The rule:

- $\Delta G < 0$ → **spontaneous** (forward);
- $\Delta G > 0$ → **nonspontaneous** (reverse favoured);
- $\Delta G = 0$ → **equilibrium**.

### Worked example
Consider a reaction with $\Delta H = +30\ \text{kJ/mol}$ (endothermic) and $\Delta S = +0.100\ \text{kJ·mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. At $T = 250\ \text{K}$: $\Delta G = 30 - (250)(0.100) = +5\ \text{kJ/mol}$ — nonspontaneous. At $T = 350\ \text{K}$: $\Delta G = 30 - (350)(0.100) = -5\ \text{kJ/mol}$ — now spontaneous. The crossover is $T = \Delta H/\Delta S = 300\ \text{K}$. Temperature is the dial that lets the entropy term win.

The four sign combinations are worth memorizing: $\Delta H<0,\ \Delta S>0$ is spontaneous at all $T$; $\Delta H>0,\ \Delta S<0$ is never spontaneous; and the two mixed cases (like our example) flip at the crossover temperature $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$.

### Why it's true / how it works
$\Delta G$ is the second law restated in a *system-only* form: at constant $T,P$, $\Delta G = -T\,\Delta S_{\text{univ}}$, so $\Delta G < 0$ is exactly $\Delta S_{\text{univ}} > 0$. $\Delta G$ also equals the maximum *useful* (non-expansion) work a process can deliver.

At equilibrium the *instantaneous* $\Delta G$ (not $\Delta G^\circ$) is zero, because the system has reached the bottom of its free-energy valley and any further change in either direction would raise $G$. Away from standard conditions, $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ tracks how far the system sits from that valley floor.

### Where it connects
Gibbs energy is the hinge of chemical thermodynamics: it links to equilibrium through $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ and to **electrochemistry** through $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$. It combines **enthalpy** and **entropy**.

### Watch out
Keep units consistent — $\Delta H$ is often in kJ but $\Delta S$ in J/K; convert before subtracting. And $\Delta G$ predicts *whether* a reaction can go, not *how fast* — a hugely favourable reaction (diamond → graphite) can be infinitely slow.

Don't confuse $\Delta G$ (depends on actual conditions, drives the reaction toward equilibrium) with $\Delta G^\circ$ (a fixed reference value tied to $K$) — using one where the other belongs is a frequent and costly error.

atoms.title: Chemical equilibrium and K
atoms.summary: A reversible reaction settles at a ratio of products to reactants fixed by the equilibrium constant K.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Many reactions never fully finish. Instead they reach a steady mixture of leftover reactants and freshly made products and then sit there, seemingly unchanged. This balance point is **equilibrium**, and $K$ is a single number telling you where it lands — mostly products, mostly reactants, or in between.

### Precisely
A reversible reaction runs forward and backward at once. At **equilibrium** the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stop changing (though molecules keep reacting both ways — it is **dynamic**). The **equilibrium constant** is
$$K = \frac{[\text{products}]}{[\text{reactants}]}\bigg|_{\text{eq}},$$
each concentration raised to its coefficient. Large $K$ favours products; small $K$ favours reactants. To predict the direction of a non-equilibrium mixture, compute the **reaction quotient** $Q$ (same ratio, current values) and compare to $K$.

### Worked example
For $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3}$,
$$K = \frac{[\mathrm{NH_3}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2}][\mathrm{H_2}]^3}.$$
Suppose at some moment $Q = 50$ while $K = 10$. Since $Q > K$, there is "too much product," so the reaction runs **in reverse**, consuming $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and rebuilding $\mathrm{N_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2}$ until $Q$ falls to $10$.

The size of $K$ is meaningful on its own: $K \gg 1$ (say $10^{10}$) means a reaction goes essentially to completion, $K \ll 1$ (say $10^{-10}$) means it barely proceeds, and $K \approx 1$ means appreciable amounts of both reactants and products coexist at equilibrium.

### Why it's true / how it works
$K$ is fixed by thermodynamics through $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$, so it depends **only on temperature** — not on starting amounts and not on whether a catalyst is present. The forward and reverse rates equalise precisely when $Q = K$, which is the steady state the system relaxes into.

Although $K$ is set purely by thermodynamics, the *equality of forward and reverse rates* at equilibrium gives the same constant from a kinetics viewpoint: $K = k_{\text{forward}}/k_{\text{reverse}}$ for an elementary reaction — a satisfying bridge between the thermodynamic and kinetic descriptions of the same balance point.

### Where it connects
Equilibrium rests on **stoichiometry** and **Gibbs free energy**, governs **Le Chatelier** shifts, and specialises into **acid–base**, **buffer**, and **solubility** equilibria. The $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ link is its own atom.

Mastering $K$ and $Q$ unlocks every specialized equilibrium that follows — acid and base ionization, buffer action, solubility products, and complex-ion formation are all the same constant wearing different chemical clothing, governed by the identical compare-$Q$-to-$K$ logic.

### Watch out
Pure **solids and liquids** are left out of $K$ (their "concentration" is constant). And $K$ describes *where* equilibrium sits, never *how fast* it is reached — a reaction with huge $K$ can still be slow without a catalyst.

$K$ has no units in the rigorous (activity-based) definition, and its numerical value depends on how the equation is written — reverse the reaction and $K$ becomes $1/K$; double the coefficients and $K$ is squared.

To predict which way a mixture that's not yet at equilibrium will move, you compute the reaction quotient Q (the same ratio using the current amounts) and compare it to K: the reaction shifts in whichever direction brings Q toward K.

atoms.title: Le Chatelier's principle
atoms.summary: A system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that partially offsets the change.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A reaction sitting at equilibrium acts like a stubborn seesaw: push on it and it pushes back. Dump in more of one ingredient and the reaction uses some of it up; take something away and it makes more. It always shifts in the direction that partly undoes whatever you did.

### Precisely
**Le Chatelier's principle**: a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting to partially offset it. Three common disturbances:

- **Concentration** — add reactant → shift toward products (remove product → same).
- **Pressure** (gases) — compress → shift toward the side with **fewer** gas molecules.
- **Temperature** — treat heat as a reactant (endothermic) or product (exothermic); adding heat shifts *away* from it.

The system settles into a **new** equilibrium, not the original.

### Worked example
For the exothermic ammonia synthesis $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3}$ (heat is a product), what happens on **raising the temperature**? Adding heat shifts equilibrium **toward reactants**, decreasing $\mathrm{NH_3}$ yield, and $K$ itself **decreases**. This is why industrial ammonia production uses moderate temperature plus **high pressure** (to favour the $2$-molecule product side over the $4$-molecule reactant side) and a catalyst for speed.

Removing a product drives a reaction forward, which industry exploits constantly: continuously condensing and drawing off ammonia in the Haber process keeps shifting equilibrium toward more $\mathrm{NH_3}$, squeezing extra yield from each pass over the catalyst.

### Why it's true / how it works
The principle is shorthand for how $Q$ is nudged relative to $K$. Changing concentration or pressure moves $Q$ while $K$ stays fixed, so the reaction re-balances $Q$ back to $K$. Only **temperature** actually changes $K$ (through $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ and the van't Hoff relation). A **catalyst** speeds forward and reverse equally — faster equilibrium, no shift.

The pressure rule follows from the same $Q$-versus-$K$ logic: compressing a gas mixture raises every partial pressure, but it raises $Q$ unequally between the two sides, and the side with fewer gas molecules relieves the increase fastest — so equilibrium shifts there to bring $Q$ back to $K$.

### Where it connects
Le Chatelier applies the logic of **chemical equilibrium** and connects to **Gibbs free energy** and the temperature dependence of $K$. It guides real process design (the Haber–Bosch process).

The principle is the everyday, qualitative companion to the more rigorous thermodynamic treatment ($\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ and the van't Hoff relation), and it is the reasoning chemists actually use at the bench and in industrial design to decide how to nudge a reaction toward more product.

### Watch out
Adding an **inert gas** at constant volume does *not* shift the equilibrium (partial pressures of the reactants are unchanged). And only changes in the count of *gas* molecules matter for the pressure effect — solids and liquids don't count.

The principle is qualitative and occasionally misleads in tricky cases; when in doubt, fall back on the rigorous comparison of the reaction quotient $Q$ to $K$, which never fails.

(2) Pressure — compress a gas mixture and equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules, easing the squeeze. Importantly, the system settles into a new equilibrium, not the original one.

atoms.title: Acids and bases
atoms.summary: Brønsted acids donate protons and bases accept them, reacting through conjugate acid-base pairs.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Acids (vinegar, lemon juice) and bases (baking soda, soap) are opposites. The simplest distinction: an acid gives away hydrogen ions ($\mathrm{H^+}$, a bare proton), and a base grabs them. They always come in matched pairs — a giver and a taker — and when they meet they neutralise each other.

### Precisely
In the **Brønsted–Lowry** model an **acid** is a proton ($\mathrm{H^+}$) **donor** and a **base** is a proton **acceptor**. Donating a proton turns an acid into its **conjugate base**; accepting one turns a base into its **conjugate acid** — so they work in **conjugate pairs**. **Strong** acids donate completely in water; **weak** acids only partially, measured by the acid-dissociation constant $K_a$. The broader **Lewis** model generalises to electron-pair acceptors (acids) and donors (bases).

### Worked example
When bicarbonate acts as an acid:
$$\mathrm{HCO_3^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + CO_3^{2-}}.$$
$\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$ donates a proton, so its **conjugate base** is **carbonate**, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$. The same bicarbonate can also act as a base ($\mathrm{HCO_3^- + H^+ \rightarrow H_2CO_3}$), making it **amphoteric** — able to donate *or* accept a proton depending on its partner.

Strength and conjugates link up neatly: hydrochloric acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$) is a strong acid that fully ionizes, so its conjugate base $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is essentially *non*-basic; acetic acid is weak, so its conjugate base (acetate) is appreciably basic — the weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base.

### Why it's true / how it works
Acid strength is the equilibrium position of proton transfer, captured by $K_a$ (often reported as $\mathrm{p}K_a = -\log K_a$; lower $\mathrm{p}K_a$ = stronger acid). A strong acid has a *weak* conjugate base and vice versa. For any conjugate pair, $K_a \cdot K_b = K_w$, the water constant. Water itself is amphoteric and self-ionises slightly even when pure.

Water's amphoterism drives its **autoionization**, $\mathrm{2H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + OH^-}$, with the tiny equilibrium constant $K_w = 1.0\times10^{-14}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ — the relation that ties $K_a$ and $K_b$ of any conjugate pair together as $K_a K_b = K_w$.

### Where it connects
Acid–base chemistry is a special case of **chemical equilibrium**, leads directly into the **pH scale**, **buffers**, and **titration**, and the Lewis extension underlies **coordination complexes** (ligands as electron-pair donors).

From this single proton-transfer idea grows a large and practical branch of chemistry — the pH scale, buffers that stabilize blood and reagents, titrations that quantify unknowns, and the Lewis extension that reaches into coordination and organic reaction mechanisms.

### Watch out
$\mathrm{H^+}$ in water is really the hydronium ion $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ — the lone proton never floats free. And "strong" vs. "concentrated" are different: a dilute strong acid is still fully dissociated, while a concentrated weak acid is still only partly so.

The Lewis definition is broader than Brønsted–Lowry, not a replacement: every Brønsted acid is a Lewis acid, but reactions with no transferable proton (like $\mathrm{BF_3}$ accepting an electron pair) are Lewis acid–base chemistry only.

atoms.title: pH and the water equilibrium
atoms.summary: pH is a logarithmic measure of hydrogen-ion concentration, with the water autoionization product fixing the neutral point.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
pH is the familiar $0$-to-$14$ ruler for how acidic or basic something is. Low numbers (lemon juice near $2$) are strong acids and taste sour; $7$ in the middle is neutral, like pure water; high numbers (bleach near $13$) are strong bases and feel slippery. Each step is a tenfold change — pH $3$ is ten times more acidic than pH $4$.

### Precisely
Acidity is set by the hydrogen-ion concentration $[\mathrm{H^+}]$. Because it spans an enormous range, we compress it logarithmically:
$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}].$$
Pure water self-ionises, and the product is fixed:
$$K_w = [\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.0\times10^{-14}\ (\text{at } 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}),$$
so $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14$. Below $7$ is acidic, $7$ neutral, above $7$ basic.

### Worked example
A solution has $[\mathrm{H^+}] = 1.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{M}$. Then
$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.0\times10^{-3}) = 3.$$
Since $3 < 7$, it is **acidic**. Its $[\mathrm{OH^-}] = K_w/[\mathrm{H^+}] = 10^{-14}/10^{-3} = 10^{-11}\ \text{M}$, giving $\mathrm{pOH} = 11$, and indeed $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 3 + 11 = 14$.

A basic solution works through $K_w$: if $[\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.0\times10^{-2}\ \text{M}$, then $[\mathrm{H^+}] = 10^{-14}/10^{-2} = 10^{-12}\ \text{M}$, so $\mathrm{pH} = 12$ (and $\mathrm{pOH} = 2$, with $\mathrm{pH}+\mathrm{pOH}=14$). Strongly basic, as expected for that much hydroxide.

### Why it's true / how it works
The logarithm turns multiplicative concentration changes into additive pH steps, which is why one pH unit is a factor of ten in $[\mathrm{H^+}]$. $K_w$ depends on temperature, so "neutral pH $= 7$" holds *only* at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; at higher temperature water self-ionises more and the neutral point drops below $7$ (still neutral, with equal $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$).

Because the scale is logarithmic, each unit is a *tenfold* change and a difference of three pH units is a *thousandfold* change in acidity — which is why small-looking pH shifts in blood or soil can have outsized chemical and biological consequences.

### Where it connects
The pH scale specialises **acid–base** equilibria and is the foundation for **buffers** and **titration**. The logarithm is the same math used in the **Nernst** and **Clausius–Clapeyron** relations.

Because so much chemistry and biology is acid–base sensitive, pH is among the most measured quantities in any lab, and it threads forward into buffers, titration curves, solubility that depends on acidity, and the ion-selective electrodes that read it electrochemically.

### Watch out
"Neutral" means equal $[\mathrm{H^+}]$ and $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$, which equals pH $7$ only at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ — don't assume $7$ is universally neutral. Strictly, pH uses hydrogen-ion *activity*, so measured pH drifts from $-\log[\mathrm{H^+}]$ in concentrated solutions.

pH can legitimately fall below $0$ or rise above $14$ for very concentrated strong acids or bases — the $0$–$14$ range is the *common* span for dilute aqueous solutions, not a hard limit. A related slip is treating pOH as an afterthought: in basic solutions it is often easier to compute pOH from the hydroxide concentration first and then use $\mathrm{pH}+\mathrm{pOH}=14$ to recover the pH.

Each step on the ruler is a tenfold change — pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.

atoms.title: Buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
atoms.summary: A weak acid and its conjugate base together resist pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A buffer is a chemical shock absorber for acidity. It keeps both an acid and its partner base on hand at once, so whatever you splash in — extra acid or extra base — gets soaked up, and the pH barely budges. Your blood is buffered this way, which is why its acidity stays remarkably steady.

### Precisely
A **buffer** resists pH change. It is a **weak acid** $\mathrm{HA}$ together with its **conjugate base** $\mathrm{A^-}$ in comparable amounts: added acid is mopped up by $\mathrm{A^-}$, added base is neutralised by $\mathrm{HA}$. Its pH follows the **Henderson–Hasselbalch equation**:
$$\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}.$$
A buffer is most effective when $[\mathrm{A^-}]\approx[\mathrm{HA}]$, i.e. when $\mathrm{pH} \approx \mathrm{p}K_a$.

### Worked example
A buffer made from acetic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a = 4.7$) with **equal** amounts of acid and acetate. Then
$$\mathrm{pH} = 4.7 + \log\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]} = 4.7 + \log(1) = 4.7 + 0 = 4.7.$$
Add a little strong acid: some $\mathrm{A^-}$ converts to $\mathrm{HA}$, nudging the ratio slightly but moving pH only a fraction of a unit — far less than the same acid would move plain water.

To shift the buffer's pH, change the ratio: an acetate buffer with three times as much base as acid sits at $\mathrm{pH} = 4.7 + \log(3) \approx 4.7 + 0.48 = 5.2$ — still near $\mathrm{p}K_a$, which is why useful buffers are chosen with a $\mathrm{p}K_a$ within about a unit of the target pH.

### Why it's true / how it works
A buffer's **capacity** — how much acid or base it absorbs before failing — is finite and peaks when $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a$, staying effective within roughly $\pm 1$ pH unit. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is an approximation valid when buffer concentrations greatly exceed the amount of acid or base added (so the ratio shifts only a little).

Blood's carbonic-acid/bicarbonate buffer ($\mathrm{H_2CO_3}/\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$) holds plasma near pH $7.4$ and is *open*: the lungs adjust $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (hence $\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$) and the kidneys adjust $\mathrm{HCO_3^-}$, giving the body two independent knobs to defend that pH.

### Where it connects
Buffers apply **acid–base** equilibria and the **pH scale**, and the **half-equivalence point** of a **titration** is exactly a $1{:}1$ buffer where $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a$. Blood's bicarbonate buffer is the biological exemplar.

### Watch out
A buffer fails once you overwhelm it — push past its capacity and pH lurches. And to make a buffer you need a *weak* acid with its conjugate base; mixing a strong acid with a strong base just neutralises to salt and buffers nothing.

At the extremes of the ratio the Henderson–Hasselbalch approximation degrades, and once added acid or base exceeds the smaller buffer component the buffer is exhausted and pH swings sharply — buffering is finite, not unlimited.

A buffer works best when that ratio is near 1, which happens when the pH is close to the pK_a.

The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is an approximation, valid when the buffer's concentrations are much larger than the amount of acid or base added. This chemistry is the operational backbone of blood pH control (the carbonic-acid/bicarbonate system) and of nearly every biochemistry experiment, where keeping pH constant is essential.

atoms.title: Reaction rate and rate laws
atoms.summary: The speed of a reaction depends on concentrations raised to experimentally determined orders.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Some reactions finish in a flash, others crawl for years. How fast one runs usually depends on how crowded the reactants are. But you cannot guess the exact relationship — doubling a reactant might double the speed, quadruple it, or change nothing. You must measure it.

### Precisely
The **reaction rate** is how fast reactants convert to products. A **rate law** links rate to concentrations:
$$\text{rate} = k[A]^m[B]^n,$$
where $k$ is the **rate constant** (specific to the reaction and temperature) and $m, n$ are the **reaction orders**. Crucially, the orders are found **experimentally**, not from the balanced equation's coefficients, because they reflect the **mechanism**. The overall order is $m + n$.

### Worked example
A reaction is **first order in A** ($m = 1$). If $[A]$ doubles, rate $\propto [A]^1$ also doubles. Suppose instead the data show rate quadruples when $[A]$ doubles — then $2^m = 4$, so $m = 2$: the reaction is **second order** in A, even if the balanced equation showed a coefficient of $1$. This is why you read orders off experiments, not equations.

The method of initial rates extracts orders cleanly: run the reaction at two starting concentrations of A (holding B fixed) and see how the rate responds — if doubling $[A]$ leaves the rate unchanged, the order in A is $0$; if it doubles, order $1$; if it quadruples, order $2$.

### Why it's true / how it works
The rate law mirrors the **rate-determining (slowest) step** of the mechanism, so the measured order encodes information about that step. A **first-order** reaction has a constant half-life $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$, independent of concentration — the same mathematics as radioactive decay. A **second-order** reaction's half-life instead grows longer as reactants thin out.

Integrated rate laws turn these orders into testable straight-line plots: for first order, $\ln[A]$ versus time is linear; for second order, $1/[A]$ versus time is linear; for zero order, $[A]$ itself is linear. Whichever plot is straight reveals the order from a single run.

### Where it connects
Rate laws build on **stoichiometry**, lead into the **Arrhenius** temperature dependence and **catalysis**, and are explained at the molecular level by **reaction mechanisms**. They are independent of thermodynamics — kinetics answers "how fast," not "how far."

Kinetics stands deliberately apart from thermodynamics: a reaction can be wildly favorable yet immeasurably slow, so rate laws answer a question equilibrium constants cannot — and that separation is why catalysis, mechanism, and the Arrhenius temperature dependence form their own pillar of the subject.

### Watch out
The cardinal error is reading orders from stoichiometric coefficients — they match only for genuine **elementary** steps. And a large $K$ (favourable equilibrium) says nothing about rate; fast and favourable are separate questions.

A zero-order reaction proceeds at a constant rate *regardless* of concentration — common when a surface or enzyme is saturated — so don't assume more reactant always means faster; sometimes the bottleneck is elsewhere.

But you can't guess the exact relationship — doubling a reactant might double the speed, or quadruple it, or change nothing at all. You have to measure it in the lab.
depths.core: Reaction rate is how fast reactants turn into products. A rate law is the equation that links that speed to the concentrations of the reactants: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. Here k is the rate constant (a number specific to the reaction and temperature), and the exponents m and n are the reaction orders — they say how sensitive the rate is to each reactant. Crucially, the orders are found by experiment, not read off the balanced equation's coefficients, because they reflect the actual step-by-step pathway (the mechanism). 'Integrated' rate laws then predict how concentration drops over time and give each reaction order a characteristic fingerprint, such as how its half-life behaves.

A first-order reaction has a constant half-life (t½ = ln2/k) that doesn't depend on concentration — the very same mathematics as radioactive decay. A second-order reaction's half-life instead grows longer as the reaction proceeds and reactants thin out.

atoms.title: Activation energy and the Arrhenius equation
atoms.summary: The rate constant grows exponentially with temperature as more molecules clear the activation-energy barrier.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Even a "downhill" reaction often needs a running start — a hill it must clear before rolling down the other side. That hill is why a log doesn't burst into flame on its own but does once a match supplies a spark. Heating the molecules gives more of them enough energy to clear the hill, so the reaction speeds up dramatically.

### Precisely
Most reactions have an energy barrier, the **activation energy** $E_a$ — the minimum energy reactants need to reach the high-energy **transition state**, after which they tumble into products. The **Arrhenius equation** gives the rate constant:
$$k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT},$$
where $A$ is the frequency factor and $e^{-E_a/RT}$ is the fraction of molecules with at least $E_a$ of energy at temperature $T$ ($R$ = gas constant). Because that fraction is exponential, small temperature rises boost the rate steeply.

### Worked example
To extract $E_a$ from data, take logarithms:
$$\ln k = \ln A - \frac{E_a}{R}\cdot\frac{1}{T}.$$
Plot $\ln k$ against $1/T$ and you get a straight line of slope $-E_a/R$. If measurements give a slope of $-6000\ \text{K}$, then $E_a = -R\times(-6000) = (8.314)(6000) \approx 50{,}000\ \text{J/mol} = 50\ \text{kJ/mol}$.

A handy rule of thumb falls out of the exponential: near room temperature, many reactions roughly *double* in rate for every $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ rise — a direct consequence of how steeply $e^{-E_a/RT}$ responds to temperature for typical activation energies.

### Why it's true / how it works
The exponential term is the **Boltzmann tail** from **kinetic-molecular theory** — the small fraction of collisions energetic enough to react. The frequency factor $A$ folds in how often molecules collide *and* the geometric requirement that they be oriented correctly. A modest temperature rise sharply enlarges the energetic tail, hence the rapid rate increase.

The reaction-coordinate diagram makes the two energies distinct: $E_a$ is the height of the hump (reactant $\to$ transition state, controlling *rate*), while $\Delta H$ is the net drop from reactants to products (controlling *heat*). A catalyst lowers the hump without touching the endpoints.

### Where it connects
Arrhenius builds on **reaction rate** and **kinetic-molecular theory**, underlies **catalysis** (lowering $E_a$), and shares its mathematical form with the **Clausius–Clapeyron** and van't Hoff equations — all rooted in Boltzmann statistics.

The activation-energy picture is also the gateway to catalysis and enzyme action, which work precisely by lowering $E_a$, and its straight-line $\ln k$-versus-$1/T$ analysis is one of the most-used experimental tools in all of chemical kinetics.

### Watch out
$E_a$ is a **kinetic** barrier, entirely separate from $\Delta H$ (the thermodynamic energy difference) — a reaction can be exothermic yet slow, or endothermic yet fast. And $T$ must be in kelvin in the exponent.

Increasing temperature speeds *both* the forward and reverse reactions, just by different amounts — so heating a reversible reaction changes its rate and can shift its equilibrium, but it never simply "pushes" it one way for free.

That hill is why a log doesn't burst into flame on its own but does once you light a match. Heating the molecules gives them more energy, so many more of them can clear the hill, and the reaction speeds up dramatically.
depths.core: Most reactions have an energy hill called the activation energy, E_a — the minimum energy reactants must gather to reach the high-energy 'transition state' at the top, after which they tumble into products. The Arrhenius equation, k = A·e^(−E_a/RT), gives the rate constant k as a frequency factor A multiplied by e^(−E_a/RT), which is the fraction of molecules that have at least E_a worth of energy at temperature T (R is the gas constant). Because that fraction sits in an exponential, even a small rise in temperature can boost the rate enormously.

Taking the logarithm shows that plotting ln k against 1/T gives a straight line of slope −E_a/R, which is the standard experimental way to measure an activation energy. The factor A also folds in the geometric requirement that colliding molecules be lined up correctly to react.

atoms.title: Catalysis
atoms.summary: A catalyst speeds a reaction by providing a lower-energy pathway without being consumed.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A catalyst is a helper that makes a reaction go faster without being used up. Picture it opening a shortcut over a smaller hill instead of the big one. Because it emerges unchanged, the same small amount helps over and over. A car's catalytic converter and the enzymes in your body both work this way.

### Precisely
A **catalyst** speeds a reaction by offering an alternative pathway with a **lower activation energy** $E_a$. It accelerates forward and reverse equally and is **regenerated**, not consumed, so a tiny amount processes large quantities of starting material. Three types: **homogeneous** (same phase as reactants), **heterogeneous** (solid catalyst, reactants on its surface), and **enzymatic** (biological catalysts — enzymes).

### Worked example
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly: $2\mathrm{H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2}$. Add a pinch of $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ (a heterogeneous catalyst) and it fizzes vigorously. The $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ provides a lower-$E_a$ surface route; via the Arrhenius factor $e^{-E_a/RT}$, even a modest drop in $E_a$ multiplies the rate enormously. Crucially, the $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ is recovered unchanged afterward — it catalysed, not reacted away.

Enzymes push this to extremes: catalase, the enzyme that handles hydrogen peroxide in your cells, accelerates its decomposition by a factor of around $10^{12}$ over the uncatalyzed rate, turning a sluggish reaction into one that finishes essentially instantly — far beyond what $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ achieves.

### Why it's true / how it works
Because a catalyst lowers $E_a$ for *both* directions by the same amount, it never changes $\Delta G$ or the position of equilibrium ($K$ is untouched) — it only shortens the time to reach equilibrium. Heterogeneous catalysts work by **adsorbing** reactants and weakening their bonds; **enzymes** achieve huge speed-ups by precisely stabilising the fragile **transition state**.

Heterogeneous catalysts cycle through adsorb–react–desorb on their surface, which is why surface area matters so much — finely divided platinum or a high-surface support exposes vastly more active sites, and why catalysts can be "poisoned" when contaminants permanently block those sites.

### Where it connects
Catalysis builds directly on **activation energy and the Arrhenius equation**, connects to **chemical equilibrium** (which it cannot shift), and is central to **organic reaction types** and industrial **Le Chatelier**-driven processes (Haber–Bosch).

Catalysis is among the most economically and biologically consequential ideas in chemistry: the vast majority of industrial chemicals are made over catalysts, and essentially every reaction in a living cell is run by an enzyme, so the simple idea of lowering a barrier without being consumed underpins both industry and life.

### Watch out
A catalyst changes **rate, not yield** — it cannot move equilibrium or make a nonspontaneous ($\Delta G > 0$) reaction go. And it is not consumed, so it never appears in the overall balanced equation.

Because a catalyst can't move equilibrium, it can never improve the *maximum* yield of a reversible reaction — it only helps you reach that ceiling faster. To raise the ceiling you must change temperature, pressure, or concentrations (Le Chatelier).

Because the catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged, the same little bit can help over and over. The catalytic converter in a car and the enzymes in your body all work this way.
depths.core: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy (a smaller energy hill to climb). It speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, and it is regenerated rather than consumed — so a tiny amount can process huge quantities of starting material (substrate). There are three flavors: homogeneous catalysis (catalyst in the same phase as the reactants, e.g. all dissolved in liquid), heterogeneous catalysis (a solid catalyst with reactants flowing over its surface), and enzymatic catalysis (biological catalysts — enzymes — in living things).

Heterogeneous catalysts work by grabbing (adsorbing) reactant molecules onto their surface and weakening their bonds. Enzymes achieve their staggering speed-ups by precisely stabilizing the transition state, the fragile high-energy arrangement at the top of the hill.

atoms.title: Oxidation–reduction reactions
atoms.summary: Redox reactions transfer electrons, with one species oxidized (losing electrons) and another reduced (gaining them).
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A whole family of reactions is really about electrons being passed from one atom to another. The atom that gives electrons away is **oxidised**; the atom that takes them is **reduced**. You can never have one without the other — every giver needs a taker. Rusting, burning, and the reactions in a battery are all electron-passing.

### Precisely
A **redox** (reduction–oxidation) reaction transfers electrons. **Oxidation** is loss of electrons (oxidation state rises); **reduction** is gain (oxidation state falls). They always occur together. The memory aid is **OIL RIG** — *Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain*. Chemists track electron flow with **oxidation numbers** and balance redox by splitting it into two **half-reactions**, conserving both atoms and charge.

### Worked example
$$\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}.$$
Split into half-reactions: oxidation $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$ (zinc goes $0\to+2$, **loses** $2e^-$, is **oxidised**); reduction $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$ (copper goes $+2\to 0$, **gains** $2e^-$, is **reduced**). The $2e^-$ released by zinc are exactly those captured by copper — electrons are conserved.

Combustion is redox too: in $\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \to CO_2 + 2H_2O}$, carbon is oxidized (its oxidation state climbs from $-4$ in methane to $+4$ in $\mathrm{CO_2}$) while oxygen is reduced (from $0$ in $\mathrm{O_2}$ to $-2$), and the electrons "lost" by carbon are exactly those "gained" by oxygen.

### Why it's true / how it works
Balancing redox conserves atoms *and* electric charge; in aqueous acid or base you also balance with $\mathrm{H^+}$, $\mathrm{OH^-}$, and $\mathrm{H_2O}$. **Oxidation state** is a formal device — imagine giving each bond's shared electrons entirely to the more electronegative atom — so it isn't a real physical charge, but it reliably tracks electron flow because every electron lost by one atom is gained by another.

The half-reaction method enforces both conservation laws step by step: balance atoms other than O and H, add $\mathrm{H_2O}$ for oxygen, $\mathrm{H^+}$ for hydrogen, then add electrons to balance charge — and finally scale the two halves so the electrons lost equal the electrons gained before adding them.

### Where it connects
Redox builds on **electron configuration** and **oxidation states**, powers **electrochemical cells** and the **Nernst equation**, and runs combustion, corrosion, respiration, and **organic** oxidations/reductions.

Redox is one of chemistry's great unifying threads, tying together combustion, corrosion, batteries, electroplating, photosynthesis, and cellular respiration — all of them, at heart, controlled transfers of electrons from one species to another.

### Watch out
Don't conflate "oxidation" with "reaction with oxygen" — oxygen is common but not required (e.g. $\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+}}$ has none). And the **oxidising agent** is the species that gets *reduced* (it causes oxidation in the other) — a frequent reversal.

Remember the agents are crossed: the species that is *oxidized* is the *reducing* agent (it donates electrons), and the one *reduced* is the *oxidizing* agent — naming them backward is one of the most common redox mistakes.

atoms.title: Electrochemical cells
atoms.summary: Separating the half-reactions of a redox process lets electron flow do electrical work, linking cell voltage to free energy.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
In a redox reaction electrons jump from one atom to another. The trick behind every battery: separate the electron-giver and electron-taker into two compartments connected only by a wire. Now the electrons must travel through the wire to cross — and electrons moving through a wire *is* electricity. You have built a battery.

### Precisely
An **electrochemical cell** harnesses a redox reaction for electricity. In a **galvanic cell** (battery), **oxidation** happens at the **anode** and **reduction** at the **cathode**; electrons flow anode → cathode through an external wire (the current), driven by the **cell potential** $E^\circ$. The bridge to thermodynamics:
$$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ,$$
where $n$ = moles of electrons transferred and $F = 96{,}485\ \text{C/mol}$ (Faraday's constant). $E^\circ > 0 \Rightarrow \Delta G^\circ < 0$ → spontaneous.

### Worked example
A zinc–copper (Daniell) cell: anode $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$ ($E^\circ_{\text{ox}} = +0.76\ \text{V}$), cathode $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$ ($E^\circ_{\text{red}} = +0.34\ \text{V}$). Cell potential $E^\circ = 0.34 + 0.76 = 1.10\ \text{V}$. With $n = 2$,
$$\Delta G^\circ = -(2)(96{,}485)(1.10) \approx -2.1\times10^{5}\ \text{J/mol} = -212\ \text{kJ/mol},$$
strongly negative — the cell drives current spontaneously.

Cell notation compactly records the Daniell cell as $\mathrm{Zn}\,|\,\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\,\|\,\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\,|\,\mathrm{Cu}$, with the anode on the left, the cathode on the right, single bars for phase boundaries, and the double bar for the salt bridge — a convention every electrochemistry problem assumes.

### Why it's true / how it works
Faraday's constant is the charge of one mole of electrons, so $nF$ converts a per-electron voltage into energy per mole, giving $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$. An **electrolytic cell** runs this in reverse: an external voltage forces a nonspontaneous reaction ($E^\circ < 0$), as in electroplating and aluminium refining. A **salt bridge** lets ions flow to keep each compartment neutral so current can continue.

Standard reduction potentials are all measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, defined as exactly $0\ \text{V}$. A cell's $E^\circ$ is the cathode's reduction potential minus the anode's, and a positive result confirms the chosen direction is the spontaneous one.

### Where it connects
Electrochemical cells unite **redox** and **Gibbs free energy**, and lead to the **Nernst equation** for non-standard conditions. They are the chemistry of batteries, fuel cells, and corrosion.

### Watch out
Anode and cathode are defined by the *process* (oxidation vs. reduction), not by sign — in a galvanic cell the anode is negative, but in an electrolytic cell it is positive. And $n$ is the electrons *transferred per reaction as written*; get it wrong and $\Delta G^\circ$ scales wrongly.

Potentials are *intensive* — they do not scale with the amount of substance, so when you multiply a half-reaction to balance electrons you must **not** multiply its $E^\circ$. (Energy $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ does scale, through $n$.)

Now the electrons have to travel through the wire to get across — and electrons moving through a wire is electricity. You've built a battery.

In a galvanic cell (a battery), oxidation and reduction are physically separated: oxidation happens at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Electrons released at the anode are forced through an external wire to the cathode, and that flow is the current; the push driving it is the voltage, called the cell potential. The standard cell potential E° is calculated from tabulated 'standard reduction potentials' for each half-reaction. The bridge to thermodynamics is ΔG° = −nFE°: here n is the number of electrons transferred and F is Faraday's constant. A positive E° gives a negative ΔG°, meaning the cell reaction is spontaneous and releases energy.

An electrolytic cell runs the same machinery in reverse: you apply an external voltage to force a nonspontaneous reaction (E° < 0) to happen, which is how metals are electroplated and aluminum is refined. A salt bridge connects the two compartments and lets ions flow to keep each side electrically neutral, so the current can keep going.

quiz.answer: The anode.

quiz.answer: A positive E° gives a negative ΔG° (since n and F are positive), so the cell reaction is spontaneous and releases energy.

atoms.title: The Nernst equation
atoms.summary: Cell potential under non-standard conditions depends on the reaction quotient through the Nernst equation.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A battery's voltage isn't fixed — it slowly sags as the chemicals inside get used up, which is why an old battery is weaker. The Nernst equation tells you exactly how the voltage depends on how much reactant is left. When everything is consumed, the voltage hits zero: the battery is dead.

### Precisely
The standard potential $E^\circ$ assumes ideal conditions (all solutes $1\ \text{M}$, all gases $1\ \text{atm}$). Real cells rarely do. The **Nernst equation** corrects for actual amounts using the reaction quotient $Q$:
$$E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q.$$
As a cell discharges, products accumulate, $Q$ rises toward $K$, and $E$ falls toward zero. A "dead" battery is simply one at equilibrium ($Q = K$, $E = 0$).

### Worked example
Relate $E^\circ$ to $K$. At equilibrium $E = 0$ and $Q = K$, so
$$0 = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln K \quad\Rightarrow\quad E^\circ = \frac{RT}{nF}\ln K.$$
At $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the prefactor simplifies and, with base-10 logs, the Nernst term becomes $\dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log Q$. So for $n=2$ and $Q=100$: $E = E^\circ - \dfrac{0.0592}{2}\log(100) = E^\circ - 0.0592\ \text{V}$.

Concentration cells run on this alone: connect two copper electrodes in $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ solutions of different concentration, and even though $E^\circ = 0$ (same half-reaction both sides), the Nernst term $-\tfrac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$ generates a small voltage that drives the system toward equal concentrations.

### Why it's true / how it works
The equation follows from $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ combined with $\Delta G = -nFE$ and $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$; dividing by $-nF$ gives the Nernst form. Setting $E = 0$ recovers the link between electrochemistry and the **equilibrium constant**.

A pH meter is a disguised Nernst device: its glass electrode develops a potential that varies linearly with pH (about $59\ \text{mV}$ per pH unit at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the $0.0592/n$ factor with $n=1$), so reading a voltage *is* reading a hydrogen-ion concentration.

### Where it connects
Nernst unites **electrochemical cells** with **chemical equilibrium**. The same equation underlies biological membrane potentials (how nerve cells fire) and the **pH electrode**, which turns an ion-concentration difference into a measurable voltage.

Its reach extends well past batteries into biology and analysis: nerve impulses, the resting potential of every cell, and the readings of pH and ion-selective electrodes are all governed by the same concentration-to-voltage relationship the Nernst equation expresses.

### Watch out
Use $T$ in kelvin and the matching $R$, and don't mix the $\ln$ form with the $0.0592/n$ form (the latter is base-10 and $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ only). $Q$ uses the *current* concentrations, not the standard-state ones.

Don't forget the logarithm is of $Q$, the *current* reaction quotient, which keeps changing as the cell runs — the voltage you measure is a snapshot, sliding toward zero as $Q$ climbs to $K$.

The Nernst equation is the formula that tells you exactly how the voltage depends on how much reactant is left. When everything is used up, the voltage hits zero: the battery is dead.

As a battery discharges, products build up, Q rises toward the equilibrium constant K, and the voltage E falls toward zero. A 'dead' battery is simply one whose reaction has reached equilibrium, where there is no longer any push.

At 25 °C the messy prefactor RT/F simplifies, so with base-10 logarithms the term becomes 0.0592/n. The same equation underlies biological membrane potentials (the voltages nerve cells use to fire) and the pH electrode, where a difference in ion concentration is turned into a measurable voltage.

atoms.title: Quantum chemistry: the Schrödinger picture of the atom
atoms.summary: Electronic structure is the set of solutions to the Schrödinger equation for electrons in the field of nuclei.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
All the dots, arrows, and orbital pictures in chemistry are really shortcuts for one deep equation from physics — a wave equation describing how electrons behave. Orbitals, chemical bonds, even the periodic table itself are just answers that fall out of solving it. Chemistry is, in a sense, what quantum physics looks like when applied to electrons around nuclei.

### Precisely
**Quantum chemistry** treats electrons as waves governed by the **Schrödinger equation**:
$$\hat{H}\psi = E\psi.$$
Here $\psi$ (psi) is the **wavefunction**, encoding where an electron is likely to be — $|\psi|^2$ gives the probability density. $\hat{H}$ (the **Hamiltonian**) is the total-energy operator, and $E$ is an allowed energy. The equation permits only certain solutions, which is why energies are **quantized**. An **orbital** is a one-electron wavefunction.

### Worked example
For the **hydrogen atom** (one electron), the equation is solved exactly. Its solutions are labelled by the quantum numbers $n, \ell, m_\ell$ and yield orbital shapes ($1s$ spherical, $2p$ dumbbell, etc.) and energies $E_n = -13.6/n^2\ \text{eV}$. The $-13.6\ \text{eV}$ ground state is the ionization energy of hydrogen — a number that drops straight out of solving $\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$, with no fitting.

The hydrogen spectrum is the equation's experimental triumph: differences between the allowed energies $E_n = -13.6/n^2\ \text{eV}$ predict the exact wavelengths of hydrogen's emission lines (the Balmer series in visible light among them), matching observation to many decimal places.

### Why it's true / how it works
Only hydrogen (one electron) is exactly solvable. Any atom or molecule with more than one electron requires approximation, because the electrons repel each other and their motions become entangled — the **electron correlation** problem. The **Hartree–Fock** method approximates this by treating each electron as moving in the *averaged* field of the others; the whole field of computational chemistry exists to approximate $\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$ for complex systems.

For many-electron systems the Hamiltonian gains electron–electron repulsion terms that couple all the coordinates together, so the equation no longer separates into one-electron pieces — this coupling is the correlation problem, and approximations like Hartree–Fock and, beyond it, configuration interaction or DFT exist precisely to tame it.

### Where it connects
This equation is the bedrock under **quantum numbers**, **molecular orbital theory**, and ultimately **computational chemistry**. Every orbital picture in the curriculum is a visualisation of one of its solutions.

### Watch out
$\psi$ itself is not directly observable and can be negative or complex — it is $|\psi|^2$ that gives a real, measurable probability. And the "orbital" is a probability cloud, not a path the electron travels.

The familiar orbital pictures are *one-electron* wavefunctions; they remain a superb language for multi-electron atoms but are an approximation there, since the true many-electron wavefunction cannot be cleanly factored into separate orbitals.

Orbitals, chemical bonds, even the whole periodic table are just answers that fall out of solving it. In other words, chemistry is what quantum physics looks like when applied to electrons around atoms.
