atoms.title: Crystal field theory
atoms.summary: Ligands around a metal ion split its d-orbitals into energy groups, explaining transition-metal color, magnetism, and stability in one picture.
atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Why is one copper solution blue and another green? Why are some iron complexes strongly magnetic and others not? The answer is that when ligands surround a transition-metal ion, they push on its $d$-orbitals unevenly, splitting a single energy level into groups. The size of that split controls color and magnetism.

### Precisely
**Crystal field theory** treats ligands as point negative charges that repel the metal's $d$-electrons. In the common **octahedral** geometry, the five $d$-orbitals split into a lower set of three ($t_{2g}$, pointing *between* ligands) and an upper set of two ($e_g$, pointing *at* ligands). The energy gap is the **crystal field splitting** $\Delta_o = E(e_g) - E(t_{2g})$. Electrons fill these levels balancing $\Delta_o$ against the **pairing energy** $P$: if $\Delta_o < P$ they spread out (**high spin**, more unpaired electrons); if $\Delta_o > P$ they pair up in the lower set first (**low spin**).

### Worked example
An octahedral $d^6$ ion like $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ can go two ways. With weak-field ligands ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, small $\Delta_o$) it is high spin: $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$, four unpaired electrons, paramagnetic. With strong-field ligands ($\mathrm{CN^-}$, large $\Delta_o$) it is low spin: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$, zero unpaired electrons, diamagnetic. Same ion, opposite magnetism — decided entirely by $\Delta_o$ versus $P$.

### Why it works
The geometry of the $d$-orbitals does the work: $d_{z^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ ($e_g$) point directly along the axes toward the six octahedral ligands, so their electrons feel more repulsion and rise in energy, while $d_{xy}, d_{xz}, d_{yz}$ ($t_{2g}$) point between ligands and are pushed less. The magnitude of $\Delta_o$ grows with ligand field strength (the **spectrochemical series**: $\mathrm{I^- < \dots < H_2O < \dots < CN^- < CO}$) and with metal oxidation state.

### Where it connects
Crystal field theory refines the **coordination-complexes** picture and is the electrostatic cousin of **molecular-orbital theory** (ligand field theory adds covalency to the same splitting). It explains transition-metal **color** — a $d$-electron absorbs a photon of energy $\Delta_o$ to jump $t_{2g}\to e_g$, so the complex shows the complementary color — and their magnetism, hydration energies, and even biological metal sites like hemoglobin's iron.

### A second angle
Because the absorbed photon energy equals $\Delta_o$, color is a direct readout of the splitting: strong-field ligands (large $\Delta_o$) absorb higher-energy, shorter-wavelength light. Change the ligands on a metal and you change $\Delta_o$ and thus the color — the visible chemistry behind indicator dyes and gemstone hues (ruby vs emerald are both $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ in different fields).

### Watch out
The splitting *pattern* depends on geometry: **tetrahedral** complexes split the *opposite* way (the $e$ set below $t_2$) and with a smaller gap ($\Delta_t \approx \tfrac49\Delta_o$), so tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin. Don't carry the octahedral ordering over blindly.

depths.eli5: When ligands surround a metal ion, they squeeze its d-orbitals unevenly, splitting one energy level into a lower group and an upper group. How big that split is decides what color the complex is and whether it's magnetic — which is why different copper or iron compounds look and behave so differently.
depths.core: Crystal field theory models ligands as point charges that repel a metal's d-electrons, splitting the five d-orbitals. In octahedral geometry they split into a lower t2g (three orbitals between ligands) and upper eg (two pointing at ligands), separated by Δo. Electrons fill by balancing Δo against the pairing energy: small Δo gives high spin (more unpaired electrons), large Δo gives low spin. Δo sets color (a t2g→eg jump absorbs a photon of that energy) and magnetism.
depths.deep: The eg orbitals (d_z², d_x²−y²) point along the axes at the six octahedral ligands and rise in energy; the t2g orbitals point between them and drop. Δo scales with ligand field strength (the spectrochemical series) and oxidation state. The high-spin/low-spin outcome is decided by Δo vs pairing energy P, illustrated by d⁶ Fe²⁺ going high-spin (4 unpaired, paramagnetic) with H₂O or low-spin (0 unpaired, diamagnetic) with CN⁻. Tetrahedral fields invert the pattern (e below t2) with Δt≈4/9 Δo, so they are nearly always high spin. Ligand field theory generalizes this by adding metal–ligand covalency to the electrostatic picture.

atoms.note: Tetrahedral complexes split oppositely (e below t2) with a smaller gap Δt ≈ (4/9)Δo, so they are almost always high spin.

quiz.prompt: In an octahedral complex, which d-orbital set is higher in energy and why?
quiz.answer: The eg set (d_z² and d_x²−y²) is higher because those orbitals point directly at the ligands and their electrons feel more repulsion; the t2g set points between ligands and is lower.

quiz.prompt: Explain how the same d⁶ ion can be paramagnetic in one complex and diamagnetic in another.
quiz.answer: It depends on Δo versus the pairing energy P. Weak-field ligands give small Δo (high spin, t2g⁴eg², 4 unpaired → paramagnetic); strong-field ligands give large Δo (low spin, t2g⁶eg⁰, 0 unpaired → diamagnetic).
